hints.quote: You'll need to know that there's 3 main types of hormones. There's the amine classification, that's gonna be your epinephrine, your norepinephrine. There's peptide hormones, like insulin, and steroid hormones, like estrogen or testosterone.
hints.take: Know the three classes with an example of each, and that steroids act on receptors inside the cell while peptides bind on the surface.

hints.quote: Because that lower jaw will grow in somebody who has acromegaly. The hands and the feet as well, but look for the jaw in your patients.
hints.take: Acromegaly in an adult shows the dentist a growing mandible: a bite moving from Class I to edge-to-edge or Class III, new diastemas and a large tongue.

hints.quote: I don't want to place an implant when their face and their body's still growing, because everything's going to move around that implant, but that implant's going to be stuck in that bone.
hints.take: The sex hormones of puberty fuse the growth plates; plan a young patient's implant for after growth stops.

hints.quote: The first thing they have to do when they're doing these surgeries is they have to identify the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Because if you damage that nerve, it actually affects the patient's vocal cords.
hints.take: Thyroid and parathyroid surgery puts the recurrent laryngeal nerve at risk: damage leaves a hoarse, raspy voice, usually for good.

hints.quote: Hypothyroidism is something you'll see far more frequently.
hints.take: Expect hypothyroid patients (fatigue, weight gain, macroglossia, slow healing, usually on thyroid hormone) far more often than hyperthyroid ones.

hints.quote: It is a life-threatening emergency. You'll see a high fever, you'll see a rapid heart rate, sometimes as much as 140 or higher. So if you start to see signs and symptoms of this, call 911.
hints.take: Thyroid storm: high fever, a pulse of 140 or more, agitation and delirium in uncontrolled hyperthyroidism; call 911.

hints.quote: So you need to understand the calcium metabolism side of this, and also its effects on oral and maxillofacial bone.
hints.take: Know what PTH, vitamin D and calcitonin each do, and read hyperparathyroidism on a radiograph: lost lamina dura, radiolucent brown tumors, loose teeth.

hints.quote: An increase in ACTH production stimulates melanocytes.
hints.take: He said he hadn't given the class this one, so he told them: in Addison disease low cortisol lets ACTH rise, and ACTH darkens the skin and oral mucosa.

hints.quote: Sometimes you have to give them supplemental corticosteroids after a bigger procedure. It would be best to talk with their doctor and find out how much you want to prescribe them before you do that.
hints.take: An Addison patient can't raise cortisol for surgical stress: know the crisis triggers (long surgery, infection or trauma, a missed dose) and plan extra steroid with the physician.

hints.quote: If you have a patient who has an HbA1c that's greater than 7, that means it's poorly controlled, and they're at much higher risk of failure of implants, they're higher risk of periodontal disease.
hints.take: Above 7 percent is poor control (more implant failure and periodontal disease); below 7 is well controlled, and a person without diabetes runs about 5.

hints.quote: I will warn you that some of these CGMs only read down to a certain level.
hints.take: If a patient looks hypoglycemic, check a finger-stick even when the CGM shows a number: his patient's read 53 while she was in the 30s.

hints.quote: Typically a straight glucose solution is a better option because it requires less processing through the liver and quicker increase in the blood sugar.
hints.take: Give straight glucose, not table sugar (half fructose); if oral glucose fails, IV dextrose or glucagon IM or subcutaneously, and expect a slow response on a GLP-1 drug.

hints.quote: One pack per day times how many years they've been doing it, that's how you get your pack year history. Don't forget that. You'll need to know that next year for clinic.
hints.take: Pack-years = packs per day times years smoked: one pack a day for 40 years is 40 pack-years.

hints.quote: Remember, type 2 diabetes patients are typically hyperinsulinemic, they're just not… it's not working like it's supposed to.
hints.take: In type 2 diabetes insulin is ineffective, not deficient; autoimmune beta-cell destruction is type 1.

hints.quote: Just a little… trivia tidbit.
hints.take: His aside that alcohol lowers ADH and nicotine raises it was offered as trivia; know ADH's job and diabetes insipidus instead.

hints.quote: Focus on: hormonal support of pregnancy and the role of the placenta/corpus luteum; hormonal changes associated with delivery and the postpartum period; prolactin vs. oxytocin; neuroendocrine effects of suckling; regulation of milk production and milk ejection. Key terms: hCG, progesterone, prolactin, oxytocin.
hints.take: Dr. Herr's Exam 3 study guide (no in-class review this time). It points at the second half of Dr. Madison's lecture: hCG keeping the corpus luteum making progesterone until the placenta takes over; the labor hormones, and oxytocin clamping the uterus after delivery while the fall in placental progesterone frees prolactin to make milk; prolactin makes the milk and oxytocin lets it down; suckling lowers dopamine (so prolactin rises), releases oxytocin, and the prolactin holds GnRH down. The guide doesn't list fertilization, implantation or capacitation; they stay in the hub, ranked after these.

hints.quote: One of those proteins that's really important is called ZP3. And ZP3, when the sperm recognize that, that is oftentimes going to initiate the acrosomal reaction, which means that acrosome is going to rupture and release those enzymes that we talked about on Friday.
hints.take: ZP3 on the zona pellucida sets off the acrosomal reaction; after it, the sperm binds ZP2.

hints.quote: Also, binding to that ZP2 protein stimulates what we call the cortical or zonal reaction, and that is going to cause a shedding of all the remaining proteins that are there, so that you don't have more than one sperm. You don't have polyspermia.
hints.take: Binding ZP2 starts the oocyte's second meiotic division and the cortical (zonal) reaction, which blocks polyspermy: one sperm, one egg.

hints.quote: This is the important part, is this last one. I think that's why I put it in here, is this hCG. Remember, I talked about there's certain hormones that the blasts start producing early. This is one of them. Because this is what rescues the corpus luteum.
hints.take: The trophoblasts start secreting hCG about 8 days after ovulation, and it keeps the corpus luteum from regressing.

hints.quote: hCG prevents the regression of corpus luteum, slows production of LH and FSH.
hints.take: His summary of hCG's two jobs: the corpus luteum stays alive and keeps making progesterone and estrogen, and LH and FSH stay low.

hints.quote: That corpus luteum kind of stays intact and keeps the production of the sex steroid hormones, for the first trimester. So it's responsible for most of those progesterone and estrogen production during the first trimester. At that point, we don't have a fully formed placenta, but after the first trimester, the placenta is pretty well developed, and it takes over the hormone production.
hints.take: First trimester: the corpus luteum makes most of the progesterone and estrogen; after it, the placenta takes over.

hints.quote: It's also what we measure when we do pregnancy tests, right? So it's very high, very quickly.
hints.take: A pregnancy test detects hCG, found in urine or blood about 10 to 11 days after fertilization.

hints.quote: Let's look at the main hormones that I care more about in the context of this, and that's your estrogens and your progesterone.
hints.take: Know where the pregnancy steroids come from: the placenta makes progesterone on its own and estriol only with the fetus's 17,20 desmolase.

hints.quote: Estriol, as I mentioned in the last lecture, is kind of the primary estrogen of pregnancy. So estradiol, just normal menstrual cycle estrogen. Estrone is menopause. Estriol is the predominant estrogen during pregnancy.
hints.take: Estradiol is the cycle's estrogen, estrone menopause's, and estriol pregnancy's.

hints.quote: And then, I think the big one is that increased oxytocin secretion coming from the posterior, right? That's going to stimulate these rhythmic contractions that are important for having to move the baby from the uterus out into the world, right? But it also is important because post-delivery, these contractions continue. That helps to prevent excessive bleeding, right?
hints.take: Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary drives labor's contractions, and after delivery the continuing contractions limit bleeding.

hints.quote: What you should know is that a lot of prolactin's effects during pregnancy are inhibited. They're kind of antagonized by progesterone.
hints.take: Progesterone antagonizes prolactin in the breast during pregnancy, so full milk production waits until progesterone falls after delivery.

hints.quote: And so what you see is that prolactin sets the stage and creates all the milk products. Oxytocin is going to stimulate milk letdown.
hints.take: Prolactin makes the milk; oxytocin contracts the myoepithelial cells to let it down.

hints.quote: I think that's it from this slide. Mainly focus on this side of things. Dopamine being important.
hints.take: On the prolactin and oxytocin slide, focus on the hypothalamus: dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin release, and suckling turns the dopamine down.

hints.quote: One thing that I want to highlight: prolactin is going to also inhibit gonadotropin-releasing hormone.
hints.take: High prolactin inhibits GnRH, so LH, FSH and the sex steroids fall: the amenorrhea of breastfeeding and of hyperprolactinemia.

hints.quote: But I don't really care that you know all the different stages for my stuff. No, you don't have to know it.
hints.take: Skip the names of the cleavage stages; know that implantation happens at the blastocyst stage and that trophoblasts form its outer layer.

hints.quote: That's facilitated through adhesion molecules. I don't care that you know them. L-selectin is one of those, and there's a variety of them.
hints.take: Know that adhesion molecules attach the blastocyst and signal the trophoblasts to differentiate, not the molecules' names.

hints.quote: You can, of course, prevent sperm and egg from contacting one another. There's a variety of methods for there. I'm not going to go into that.
hints.take: He skipped the methods that keep sperm and egg apart; know the endocrine ones: the pill blunts the LH surge, progestin thickens mucus, high-dose estrogen prevents implantation.

hints.quote: Focus on: major actions of estrogens, progestins, and androgens; how hormonal contraceptives prevent pregnancy; major drug classes that alter reproductive hormone signaling; drugs that block androgen receptors or androgen metabolism; important therapeutic effects and adverse effects. Key terms: GnRH analogs, progestins, antiandrogens, 5α-reductase inhibitors.
hints.take: From Dr. Herr's study guide. For Dr. Fasinu's lecture that means each drug class by mechanism, use and main adverse effect: GnRH analogs (given continuously, they switch LH and testosterone off), the 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride), the androgen receptor antagonists (flutamide, bicalutamide), the SERMs, aromatase inhibitors and progestins; how contraceptives work (progestins suppress FSH and LH, so no ovulation; Plan B versus ulipristal); and the adverse effects he stressed, thromboembolism for the estrogens and hepatotoxicity for testosterone.

hints.quote: You want to be able to list the examples of estrogenic drugs, the SERMs, the androgenic drugs, and the anti-androgenic drugs. And if you're able to do those, the names will suggest to you how they work, based on their classes, like aromatase inhibitors, so you know they inhibit aromatase enzyme, which means that you have to know what aromatase enzyme does.
hints.take: Learn the examples in each class; the class name gives the mechanism, so know what each target enzyme or receptor does.

hints.quote: I think it's the most serious and most common side effect of estrogens.
hints.take: Thromboembolism is estrogen's signature risk: a history of a clot rules estrogen out.

hints.quote: Dihydrotestosterone is the active testosterone. That is the one that is active.
hints.take: 5-alpha-reductase bioactivates testosterone to DHT, so its inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) lower androgen activity.

hints.quote: Those who have aromatase deficiency are not able to make estradiol, and they're the ones that grow very tall, and the epiphysis doesn't close early, and they grow tall, they have weak bone, they have high risk of osteoporosis.
hints.take: Estradiol closes the epiphyses, so a man without aromatase grows tall with weak, osteoporotic bones.

hints.quote: I think the most important side effect of testosterone everyone needs to also know is hepatotoxicity. That is one big thing that people get screened for. If they already have an existing liver problem, they don't get testosterone.
hints.take: Hepatotoxicity is the testosterone side effect to know; liver disease is a contraindication.

hints.quote: If you understand your physiology, gonadotropin-releasing hormone is supposed to be pro-androgen. But because we give it exogenously, and they stimulate the cell long-term, so eventually they switch the cells off.
hints.take: Long-acting GnRH analogs (goserelin) replace the natural pulses with constant stimulation, which shuts off FSH, LH and testosterone.

hints.quote: You want to know those examples, especially your testosterone standard and the cypionate, which is the depot. I don't think I want to bother you about those other ones.
hints.take: Of the androgen drugs, know testosterone and testosterone cypionate (the IM depot); the other analogs on his table were not his focus.

hints.quote: So the difference between Proscar and Propecia is the dose, the strength of the tablet. And also for the indication. The high strength is for BPH, the low strength is for alopecia.
hints.take: Proscar and Propecia are both finasteride: the higher strength treats BPH, the lower strength hair loss.

hints.quote: These drugs, drugs that are estrogenic, even those that are anti-estrogenic, they tend to increase clotting factors, and that's why they have a problem with thrombosis.
hints.take: Estrogens raise clotting factors 2, 7, 9 and 10, and the SERMs and aromatase inhibitors share the clot risk.

hints.quote: And several other effects, very similar to testosterone. I don't want to bother you with that.
hints.take: The rest of his second estrogen-effects slide (ACTH, well-being, binding globulins, FSH and LH inhibition) was skipped; know the clotting, lipid, bone, skin and uterine effects.

hints.quote: When there's overexpression of estrogen receptor in the breast cancer cells, it suggests that the cancerous growth is being fueled by estrogens. So that means anti-estrogens will work. So that is the only time you give tamoxifen.
hints.take: Tamoxifen is for ER-positive breast cancer only.

hints.quote: So again, tamoxifen for breast cancer, raloxifene for osteoporosis, Clomid, that is for, to stimulate ovulation.
hints.take: Match each SERM to its use: tamoxifen, breast cancer; raloxifene, osteoporosis; clomiphene, ovulation.

hints.quote: Now, you have other examples there? They are rarely used.
hints.take: Toremifene, ospemifene, bazedoxifene and fulvestrant on the SERM table are rarely used; know tamoxifen, raloxifene and clomiphene.

hints.quote: At least you should be able to remember hot flashes associated with estrogens and thromboembolism.
hints.take: Aromatase inhibitors (anastrozole): remember hot flashes and thromboembolism.

hints.quote: The other differences, which is probably more important, is that Plan B has to be used within 72 hours, but ulipristal, that is your Ella, can be used up to 5 days. … The other one is that ulipristal is by prescription only, whereas you can buy Plan B without prescription.
hints.take: Plan B: levonorgestrel, within 72 hours, no prescription. Ulipristal: an antagonist, up to 5 days, prescription only.

hints.quote: Pay attention to those drugs that I highlight in the slides, and you should be fine.
hints.take: Know the red drugs: goserelin, finasteride, dutasteride, flutamide, bicalutamide, tamoxifen, raloxifene, anastrozole, progesterone, hydroxyprogesterone, levonorgestrel, ulipristal.

hints.quote: Focus on: recognition and major functions of RBCs, platelets, and leukocytes; functions of neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, monocytes, and lymphocytes; innate vs. adaptive immunity; general roles of B cells, T cells, and NK cells; primary vs. secondary lymphoid organs; basic organization and function of the thymus, lymph node, and spleen. Key terms: neutrophil, eosinophil, NK cell, thymus, bone marrow, spleen, PALS.
hints.take: Dr. Herr's guide to his own lecture, and it asks for general roles and basic organization. Recognize each blood cell and know its job: red cells carry oxygen and carbon dioxide, platelets (megakaryocyte fragments) start clotting, neutrophils kill bacteria, eosinophils fight parasites and allergy, basophils hold heparin, monocytes become macrophages. Then B cells (antibodies), T cells (CD4 helpers, CD8 killers) and NK cells; the bone marrow and thymus as primary organs versus the nodes, MALT and spleen as secondary; and the layout of the thymus (cortex, medulla), lymph node (B-cell follicles, T-cell paracortex) and spleen (white pulp with its PALS of T cells around the central arteriole, red pulp).

hints.quote: What you need to remember with white blood cells is we've got two classes and 5 types.
hints.take: Granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) have prominent granules; agranulocytes (monocytes and lymphocytes) don't.

hints.quote: Remember, platelets arise from megakaryocytes. That's just knowledge you should know, all right?
hints.take: Platelets are pieces of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow, and they take part in clotting.

hints.quote: Just think when you hear the word humoral, think B-cell response, okay? And then also, when you hear B cells, think about the production of antibodies.
hints.take: Humoral means B cells and antibodies; cellular means T cells, which target transformed cells.

hints.quote: So you know that term, plasma cell. And you can associate that with antibody production and release.
hints.take: A B cell whose antibody fits its antigen recruits helper T cells and becomes a plasma cell, which releases that antibody; in a lymph node, plasma cells secrete it in the medulla.

hints.quote: So if we look at this, this kind of schematic is pretty helpful. It's just, in general speaking, kind of what NK cells are doing in three different scenarios.
hints.take: MHC class I on a healthy cell binds the NK cell's inhibitory receptor and stops the killing; a cell missing it is killed; far more activating ligands cause induced killing.

hints.quote: We're not going to consider GALT as a primary lymphatic organ, but we will consider the thymus and the bone marrow as our primary lymphoid organs.
hints.take: The primary lymphoid organs are just the bone marrow and the thymus; any other lymphoid organ, GALT included, is secondary.

hints.quote: Since the thymus is the exception, the stroma of the thymus is composed of what's called epithelioreticular cells, and I do want you to know that. So epithelioreticular cells, you should associate that with the thymus.
hints.take: Every lymphoid organ's stroma is reticular cells and type III collagen except the thymus's, which is epithelioreticular cells.

hints.quote: The bone marrow is gonna serve as our B-cell development center, the thymus is gonna serve as our T-cell center.
hints.take: B and NK cells form and mature in the marrow; T cell precursors leave it immunoincompetent and mature in the thymus.

hints.quote: There's a lot of programmed cell death that occurs as a process of thymocyte selection. So approximately 95 to 99% of the cells that go there are going to be selected out.
hints.take: In the thymus, 95 to 99 percent of thymocytes fail selection and die by apoptosis; macrophages clear them.

hints.quote: The main thing is just to really associate this PALS with the spleen.
hints.take: The PALS, the T cell sheath around the central artery of the white pulp, means the spleen: "if you see a central artery, that's where you have that area of PALS."

hints.quote: I'm not gonna ask you any questions specifically on stained images, so you don't have to worry about those too much.
hints.take: Know each cell and region by its described features; no stained images on the exam ("there's not any images on your exam, necessarily").

hints.quote: No reason to memorize the typical concentration of cells. You can, of course, review the names and functions.
hints.take: Skip the counts per liter in his summary table; know each cell's name, share of the white count and job.

hints.quote: You don't have to memorize this huge list, we'll talk about what they're doing.
hints.take: Skip the long list of lymphoid tissues on his overview figure; know which two are primary and what the main secondary ones do.

hints.quote: And you saw that slide at the very beginning that talked about colony forming units, okay, and what they give rise to, so you don't have to worry about that next sentence, right?
hints.take: Skip the colony-forming unit names on the bone marrow slide (CFU-Ly, CFU-LyB, CFU-LyT); know what each blood cell line gives rise to.

hints.quote: The helper and cytotoxic T cells will respond slightly differently, we don't really get into it, but essentially the helper T cells are what's going to help our B lymphocytes, and the cytotoxic T cells are probably just gonna kill whatever they bind.
hints.take: Know the general roles: helper T cells help the B cells and cytotoxic T cells kill what they bind; he didn't go into how each one responds.

hints.quote: Focus on: how the major leukemias are classified; acute vs. chronic disease; myeloid vs. lymphoid disease; major differences between Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma; recognizing important lymphoma categories and associations; common clinical consequences of leukemia. Key terms: ALL, AML, CLL, CML, Reed-Sternberg cells, Burkitt lymphoma, Mantle cell lymphoma, Mycosis fungoides/Sézary syndrome.
hints.take: From Dr. Herr's study guide, for Dr. Borak's lecture. Place the four leukemias on two axes (acute or chronic, myeloid or lymphoid) and know each one's look: AML's blasts and Auer rods, ALL in young children, CML's Philadelphia chromosome, CLL's smudge cells. Know the two ways leukemia does harm (marrow failure: anemia, bleeding, infection; infiltration: spleen, liver, nodes, bone, gums), Hodgkin versus non-Hodgkin (Reed-Sternberg cells and contiguous nodes above the diaphragm, versus mostly B-cell and often extranodal), and the lymphomas by their associations: Burkitt (t(8;14), MYC, EBV, the jaw), mantle cell (t(11;14), cyclin D1), mycosis fungoides (patches, plaques, tumors) and Sézary syndrome (erythroderma, nodes, Sézary cells in the blood).

hints.quote: And then there are some key symptoms, that are called B symptoms, that are really, like, high-yield clues that this person is somebody you should be concerned about lymphoma.
hints.take: The B symptoms: a fever of 38 °C or higher, drenching night sweats that soak the sheets, and unexplained loss of at least 10 percent of body weight in 6 months; they raise the suspicion, and the tissue makes the diagnosis.

hints.quote: These are just an example of some of the antigens that are on the surface of the cell. You do not need to know this. Do not waste a second learning what these antigens are. I just want you to understand the concept, that it's telling you that it's a myeloid cell, it's a B cell, it's a T cell, and then we're looking to see if there's additionally something abnormal on the surface of the cell.
hints.take: Skip the individual CD markers; know that flow cytometry reads the surface antigens to tell B, T or myeloid, mature or blast, and something abnormal, such as a clone with only kappa or only lambda.

hints.quote: And for you guys, an important one, is that sometimes these leukemias can actually present as gingival hypertrophy and oral lesion. So you guys may actually be the clue that a patient has leukemia that's not detected.
hints.take: Swollen gums from leukemic cells growing in them can be the first sign of a leukemia nobody has found yet; with fatigue, pallor and bruising, get a blood count.

hints.quote: If you see greater than 20% blast, you can go ahead and diagnose an acute leukemia. If you see just a few, you get that bone marrow, and you may see greater than 20% blast. That's our threshold for making the diagnosis.
hints.take: Blasts are the hallmark of acute leukemia, and more than 20 percent, in the blood or the marrow, makes the diagnosis; an AML with a defining genetic abnormality needs no set count.

hints.quote: We also use cytogenetic and molecular information to do the classification, so you don't need to know any of these actual things, that's just to illustrate the concept.
hints.take: Skip the AML subtypes (M0 to M7) and the subtype lists of AML and ALL; know AML versus ALL, and the acute leukemias he named.

hints.quote: So if you got a test question, let's say this is expressing cyclin D1. You would know this is mantle cell lymphoma.
hints.take: Cyclin D1, switched on by t(11;14), means mantle cell lymphoma; he said nothing else among the lymphomas carries t(11;14).

hints.quote: The last low-grade B-cell lymphoma is the one you guys are going to experience the most. Marginal zone lymphoma.
hints.take: Marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma: indolent, in the salivary glands and ocular adnexa, linked to H. pylori, Chlamydia psittaci, Sjögren syndrome and Hashimoto thyroiditis, with lymphoepithelial lesions as its key finding.

hints.quote: So, starry sky pattern is the key morphologic finding in making this diagnosis.
hints.take: Burkitt lymphoma's starry sky is macrophages eating the debris of tumor cells that proliferate very fast; it carries t(8;14), MYC with IGH.

hints.quote: And so, that's the main thing that you need to recognize, is those Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells.
hints.take: Classic Hodgkin lymphoma is a few very large Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells, with very prominent nucleoli, scattered among reactive cells.

hints.quote: There are other types of classical Hodgkin's lymphoma, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-rich, lymphocyte depleted. That's based on the reactive background of lymphocytes, eosinophils. But you don't need to know the difference between them otherwise.
hints.take: Skip the differences between the classic Hodgkin subtypes (and the non-classical type, which he also said you don't need); recognize the Reed-Sternberg cells.

hints.quote: I'm going to skip peripheral T-cell lymphoma. These are basically very aggressive T-cell lymphomas.
hints.take: Know only the gist he gave: a very aggressive T-cell lymphoma, usually with B symptoms, that doesn't necessarily respond to chemotherapy.

hints.quote: I'm not going to go over in much detail, but know that these are the most common types of cutaneous lymphomas that are involving the skin, and that they have an indolent course.
hints.take: Mycosis fungoides: know that it is the most common lymphoma of the skin, a T-cell lymphoma with an indolent course, and that Sézary syndrome is its aggressive form, with the blood and nodes involved.

hints.quote: The main chronic leukemia that you need to know is chronic myeloid leukemia.
hints.take: CML: t(9;22), the Philadelphia chromosome and BCR-ABL1; a very high white count with every stage of maturation and few blasts; tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib.

hints.quote: Two big ones you need to know. Acute promyelocytic leukemia, which is associated with translocation 15 and 17.
hints.take: APL: t(15;17) fuses PML with RARA and stops maturation at the promyelocyte; know it for its DIC, which can kill, and for its excellent cure with all-trans retinoic acid and arsenic trioxide.

hints.quote: Another one that you need to know that I mentioned with acute monocytic leukemia, these are leukemias of the monocyte, and the thing that I want you to know is that they can have extramedullary disease presentation in the oral cavity.
hints.take: Acute monocytic leukemia can show outside the marrow in the mouth, as swollen gums infiltrated by leukemic cells.

hints.quote: You don't need to know a ton of detail other than some of the demographic information for this.
hints.take: For B-ALL and T-ALL, know who gets them: mostly children (usually 1 to 5 years, poor prognosis under 1), less often adults; T-ALL is confirmed as T-cell by testing.

hints.quote: I want you to know generally kind of what category things are. Which of these things are B-cell lymphoma? Which of these things are T-cell lymphoma? You do need to know the molecular associations on the ones that are sort of underlined and things like that. You don't need to know the flow cytometry stuff, CD5, CD33. Don't waste your time learning that kind of stuff.
hints.take: His closing summary: know each disease's category (B or T, indolent or aggressive, acute or chronic, myeloid or lymphoid) and its molecular association: t(14;18) follicular, t(11;14) mantle cell, t(8;14) Burkitt, t(9;22) CML, t(15;17) APL; not the markers.

hints.quote: Focus on: disorders of testicular development/descent; major categories of testicular tumors; common infections of the male reproductive tract; major benign and malignant prostate disorders. Key terms: cryptorchidism, germ-cell tumors, seminoma, BPH, prostatic adenocarcinoma, Gleason grading.
hints.take: From Dr. Herr's study guide, for Dr. Dal Zotto's lecture. Know cryptorchidism (why the testis has to come down: body heat halts spermatogenesis, so infertility and testicular cancer, and surgery leaves the cancer risk), the categories of testicular tumors (95 percent germ cell tumors, the rest mostly sex cord-stromal; seminoma versus non-seminomatous), the infections (syphilis, gonorrhea and chlamydia of the glans and foreskin; gonorrhea and chlamydia in epididymitis; orchitis uncommon), and the prostate: BPH around the urethra against adenocarcinoma in the peripheral zone, with PSA, osteoblastic bone metastases and Gleason grading.

hints.quote: You just need to know that the majority of urothelial carcinomas are from the urothelium, epithelial in origin. 90% arise from the urothelium, that specialized epithelium that covers all the urinary tract. ... But if you remember only that the majority of the urothelial neoplasms are located in the bladder and are urothelial carcinomas, I will be happy.
hints.take: 90 percent of urinary tract tumors are urothelial carcinomas, and most are in the bladder; squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma and mesenchymal tumors are the rest.

hints.quote: Smoking is four times... urothelial carcinomas you find more in smokers than in non-smokers, four times. And the incidence of urothelial carcinomas or bladder carcinomas did not decrease after cessation of smoking, compared with the lung cancer, that if you stop smoking, the risk goes down. For bladder, it doesn't go down. So smoking is a very strong risk factor for urothelial carcinoma.
hints.take: Smoking: four times the risk of urothelial carcinoma, and quitting doesn't lower it. The other risks: dyes, rubber, leather and textiles; pelvic radiation for cervical cancer; cyclophosphamide; chronic catheters and infections; Schistosoma haematobium (squamous cell carcinoma, Egypt).

hints.quote: So remember, the lower numbers, 6 and 11, are benign. Higher numbers, 16 and 18, are premalignant, are the ones that are going to produce premalignant lesions. And, look at this number. 30% evolve to invasive carcinomas if they are not treated.
hints.take: HPV 6 and 11: condyloma acuminatum, benign and verrucous. HPV 16 and 18: penile intraepithelial neoplasia, flat and red, 30 percent invasive if untreated. The HPV-independent kind comes with lichen sclerosus in men over 60.

hints.quote: Why we separate seminoma versus non-seminoma? Because seminoma behaves very well and responds to radiotherapy. The rest of the tumors in the testicle won't respond so well. So, the clinician needs to know if this is a seminoma or a non-seminomatous tumor, and that's enough.
hints.take: The split to know: seminoma (radiosensitive, behaves very well) versus the non-seminomatous tumors (embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, teratoma), which don't respond as well.

hints.quote: Usually, seminomas are tumors of the young adults. Affect people in between 30s, 40s. So if I see a young adult with a testicular tumor myself, I'm going to think, okay, this has a high chance to be a seminoma. It's associated with cryptorchidism, the lack of testicular descent to the scrotum, and usually don't have any tumor markers that serologically the clinician can tell.
hints.take: Seminoma: the most frequent, young adults in their 30s and 40s, white, multinodular and solid with no hemorrhage or necrosis, tied to cryptorchidism, usually no serum marker (the pathologist diagnoses it).

hints.quote: Testicular tumors are a big portion of the pathology. 95% of the testicular tumors are derived from the spermatogonias, the germ cell tumors. And the rest are derived from the Sertoli cells, the Leydig cells, what we call sex cord-stromal tumors.
hints.take: 95 percent germ cell tumors, from the spermatogonia; the rest sex cord-stromal (Sertoli, Leydig) or mixed, plus lymphoma (secondary) and metastases in older men. Germ cell tumors are cured in more than 95 percent.

hints.quote: So those high temperatures halt the spermatogenesis, and can be the cause of infertility and testicular cancer. So, it needs to be corrected at 2 years old, right? Surgically corrected. Even if it's surgically corrected, infertility won't occur, but the risk of testicular cancer is still a possibility for that kid, okay?
hints.take: Cryptorchidism: an undescended testis at body temperature can't make sperm. Wait up to the second year, then surgery; surgery prevents the infertility, but the testicular cancer risk stays.

hints.quote: Two conditions, benign conditions in the testis that are relatively frequent, and both are medical emergencies.
hints.take: Testicular torsion (a twisted cord, the testis infarcts) and inguinal hernia (bowel trapped in an open inguinal canal, the bowel infarcts) are emergencies.

hints.quote: These two zones can predict the pathology. The benign prostatic hyperplasia is located around the urethra, is in the transitional zone, or the periurethral zone, and the peripheral zone is the location of the prostatic carcinomas.
hints.take: BPH around the urethra (transition zone): it obstructs the urine. Carcinoma in the peripheral zone: it doesn't obstruct early.

hints.quote: Benign prostatic hyperplasia, as I said before, is very common. Guys, you are going to have it. You cannot avoid this. After 50s, your prostate is going to start to be hyperplastic. It's going to grow. And you are going to have difficulties in urinating.
hints.take: BPH, hyperplasia of the glands and stroma, comes to nearly every man after 50 and makes urinating hard; hormones play a role, and surgery treats severe obstruction.

hints.quote: The one thing that the prostatic adenocarcinoma does very special is that it likes the bones. It likes to metastasize in bones, and that bone metastasis characteristically forms more bone. So we call it osteoblastic. When we see in a patient an osteoblastic lesion in bones, we think about prostatic adenocarcinoma. We are going to order a blood draw for PSA.
hints.take: Prostatic adenocarcinoma, the most frequent cancer in men (over 65): osteoblastic bone metastases; an osteoblastic lesion means a serum PSA.

hints.quote: And the prognosis depends on the differentiation grade. We use a grading that is called Gleason grading system that goes from the well-differentiated glands to the poorly differentiated glands, more masses of tumor and single cells.
hints.take: Gleason grades the differentiation, from well-formed glands to masses and single cells; the worse the differentiation, the worse the prognosis.

hints.quote: Okay, remember, cryptorchidism is a predisposing factor to testicular cancer. ... Phimosis is a predisposing factor to... the foreskin cannot retract, sticky into the glans, is a predisposing factor to penile carcinoma, okay? Carcinoma of the penis.
hints.take: The closing review: cryptorchidism predisposes to testicular cancer; phimosis predisposes to carcinoma of the penis.

hints.quote: And then you have weird stuff, like retroperitoneal fibrosis, forget about that.
hints.take: Skip retroperitoneal fibrosis; know stones (at the narrow spots, especially where the ureter enters the bladder) and tumors as the causes of ureteral obstruction.

hints.quote: And on the right, you can see the urinary tract tumors classifications from the WHO that you need to know for sure. No, I'm just kidding. You don't need to know that.
hints.take: Skip the WHO classification of urinary tract tumors; know that 90 percent are urothelial carcinomas, mostly in the bladder.

hints.quote: And now we know that there are two pathways of urothelial carcinomas, molecular pathways. One is the mutation of this gene, fibroblastic growth factor receptor 3, and others are the mutation of the tumor suppressor gene TP53. ... This is just your general information. You don't need to know.
hints.take: Skip FGFR3 and TP53; know papillary tumors, low versus high grade (nuclear pleomorphism), and that the depth of invasion sets the stage.

hints.quote: This is the classification. For you to know, you don't need to know this, but, the classification is going to be simple for you. As I said before, big, big, big: seminoma versus non-seminomatous tumors.
hints.take: Skip the full classification of testicular tumors; sort them into seminoma and non-seminomatous.

hints.quote: And these are the cells of the seminoma. It's... you don't need to know this, it's just for you to know that it looks like fried eggs, because the cells are vacuolated, have this clear cytoplasm.
hints.take: Skip the seminoma's look under the microscope; know its cut surface (white, solid, no hemorrhage or necrosis) and who gets it.

hints.quote: Teratomas, on the other hand, are non-seminomatous, and frequently recapitulate different mature tissues. ... But you don't need to know this, alright? It's just for you to, part of your general information.
hints.take: Skip each non-seminomatous tumor's features (embryonal carcinoma's necrosis, the yolk sac tumor's Schiller-Duval bodies, choriocarcinoma's beta-hCG, the teratoma's tissues); know them as the non-seminomatous group, more aggressive and less radiosensitive than seminoma.

hints.quote: Focus on: common disorders of the vulva, vagina, and cervix; distinguishing neoplastic from non-neoplastic lesions; important infectious causes of reproductive tract disease; relationship between HPV and cervical neoplasia; important age-related patterns of reproductive tract tumors. Key terms: lichen sclerosus, condyloma acuminatum, sarcoma botryoides, HPV, cervical neoplasia, infectious vaginitis.
hints.take: From Dr. Herr's study guide, for Dr. Dal Zotto's lecture. Know HPV and the cervix (the transformation zone, the low- and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions, 90 percent HPV, the koilocyte), the infectious vaginitis pair (Candida's pseudohyphae; Trichomonas, a sexually transmitted protozoan with prolongations) against atrophic vaginitis, the vulva's lichens (lichen sclerosus leads to HPV-independent carcinoma), condyloma acuminatum (HPV 6 and 11, benign), and the ages: sarcoma botryoides in girls under 5, squamous carcinomas in the reproductive years, lichen sclerosus carcinoma in older women.

hints.quote: And then the boundaries in between the ectocervix and the endocervix is the transformation zone. Why I'm talking about so much of this? Because that transformation zone is very important as a localization of the endocervical cancer, or the cervical cancer.
hints.take: Cervical cancer arises in the transformation zone, where the endocervix's glandular epithelium meets the ectocervix's squamous epithelium.

hints.quote: So they are going to collide, and it's what we call the fighting of epithelia. One epithelium is trying to get in, the other is trying to get out, and this area is very constantly inflamed and injured. ... That area is very susceptible to cancer. Why? Because it's susceptible to infection. And the most important infection is this guy, this virus that affects all the genital tracts in women and males: the HPV.
hints.take: The fighting of epithelia keeps the transformation zone inflamed and open to HPV, which can progress to carcinoma.

hints.quote: These lesions can be subclassified in low-grade and high grade. Low-grade have a low progression and can regress. The high grade are less likely to regress and can more likely progress to carcinomas. And all of these lesions are linked to the HPV infection. The majority, 90% of the cases, are linked to the HPV infection in reproductive age.
hints.take: Low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions can regress; high-grade ones progress. About 90 percent are linked to HPV.

hints.quote: This is the cytopathic effect of the HPV, the ones that we are looking for during cytology to say, yes, there is a squamous intraepithelial lesion in this woman. ... The cell is called the koilocyte, because it has a cavity in the middle.
hints.take: The koilocyte, a bigger nucleus with a clear halo around it, is HPV's mark in cytology and biopsies. High-grade cells: less cytoplasm, a higher N:C ratio, pleomorphic nuclei.

hints.quote: So know that there are certain tumors that affect the girls, and usually the squamous cell carcinomas affect the women in reproductive age.
hints.take: Sarcoma botryoides (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma) in girls under 5, with a good prognosis if treated in time; squamous cell carcinomas in women of reproductive age.

hints.quote: Another inflammatory non-infectious condition is lichen sclerosus, and I want to pause here because this is important. Lichen sclerosus is of unknown cause. It's postulated autoimmune disorder, but not proven yet. And the most important thing is that it predisposes to premalignant and malignant lesions in the vulva, squamous cell carcinomas of the vulva.
hints.take: Lichen sclerosus: atrophic epithelium, dermal sclerosis and hyalinization, a parchment-like vulva; it leads to the HPV-independent vulvar squamous cell carcinoma of older women.

hints.quote: But, note that lichen sclerosus is the single non-infectious inflammatory disorder that can lead to carcinomas.
hints.take: Of lichen simplex chronicus, lichen sclerosus and lichen planus, only lichen sclerosus leads to carcinoma.

hints.quote: Another non-infectious inflammatory disorder that I put here, because I'm trying to relate to the mouth, is this lichen planus. You must know about this, because you're going to be dentists. ... If the patient has vulvar lesions and oral lesions, it's most likely related to lichen planus.
hints.take: Lichen planus: oral and vulvar erosions together; a fresh biopsy (not in formalin) for immunofluorescence; steroids.

hints.quote: In the vulva, also, we have those condyloma acuminatum. Same in the penis, and same in the anogenital tract. ... and is, again, associated with HPV 6 and 11, low risk, low number, low risk, benign condition.
hints.take: Condyloma acuminatum: HPV 6 and 11, benign, finger-like and wart-like, with koilocytes. Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma: HPV 16 and 18, or, in women over 60, lichen sclerosus.

hints.quote: Within the infectious vaginitis, the fungal organisms, such as Candida, like this, pseudohyphae, what we can see here as little sticks. With a lot of inflammation in this cytology is very frequent, and the sexually transmitted Trichomonas vaginalis is a protozoan that is very easy to diagnose in cytology, because it looks like a squamous cell, but it has a prolongation, cytoplasmic prolongation, or pseudopods.
hints.take: Infectious vaginitis: Candida (pseudohyphae, little sticks) and Trichomonas vaginalis (a sexually transmitted protozoan with prolongations). Non-infectious: atrophic vaginitis in older women.

hints.quote: Just know that there are two types of carcinomas. One carcinoma that recapitulates the normal endometrium somehow. That is why we call it endometrioid adenocarcinoma. And it's associated with estrogen stimulation.
hints.take: Endometrioid adenocarcinoma: estrogen excess (obesity, estrogen without progesterone), well differentiated, less aggressive, younger women. The other type: over 65, unlike endometrium, more aggressive.

hints.quote: But usually a very frequent cause and very easy to treat cause of infertility is the chronic endometritis.
hints.take: Chronic endometritis: plasma cells in the endometrial stroma, a common cause of infertility, treated with antibiotics.

hints.quote: So know that ovarian cancer is a very frequent source of carcinoma, and it's lethal. ... it's going to be a very aggressive carcinoma and needs a lot of chemotherapy and the debulking surgery, and the prognosis is not very good for that patient.
hints.take: Most ovarian tumors are epithelial, from the surface; ovarian cancer is aggressive and lethal.

hints.quote: So, know the status of the receptors of a particular tumor, and the HER2 status of that particular tumor helps the clinician to treat with specific drugs.
hints.take: Breast carcinoma's prognosis: type, size, lymph nodes, and the estrogen and progesterone receptors and HER2, which drugs can target; anti-estrogen therapy for an estrogen-receptor tumor.

hints.quote: So whenever we see mammary Paget disease, we look for, with mammography or any other imaging studies, we look for the carcinoma in the breast. And the prognosis is determined by the carcinoma that is underlying.
hints.take: Paget disease of the nipple, a scaly red nipple of carcinoma cells, means looking for the carcinoma underneath.

hints.quote: This slide, you can skip it, but know that the cervical cancer screening in women have changed in the past 5 years. This is super new. The management or screening of a woman is now based on a risk.
hints.take: Skip the screening slide's details; know that cervical screening and management are now risk-based.

hints.quote: This is the classification of ovarian cancer. Don't shoot me. I don't need you to know this, but know that the ovary can give rise to a plethora of tumors.
hints.take: Skip the classification of ovarian tumors; know that most are epithelial (then germ cell and stromal) and that ovarian cancer is lethal.

hints.quote: This is an example of ductal carcinoma in situ. This is an example of lobular carcinoma in situ. I know that looks the same for you, for me too, sometimes, but it has a difference, you don't need to know that.
hints.take: Skip how DCIS and LCIS differ under the microscope; know that DCIS needs treatment and LCIS is now considered benign.

dental: Hormone classes: amine = epinephrine, peptide = insulin, steroid = estrogen. Steroids bind intracellular receptors.
Anterior pituitary: ACTH (adrenal cortex), TSH (thyroid), GH (growth), FSH and LH (reproduction), prolactin (lactation). Posterior: ADH (water; diabetes insipidus) and oxytocin.

GH persists for life; puberty's sex hormones fuse the growth plates (wait for growth to stop before an implant). Excess before puberty: very tall; after: acromegaly, a growing mandible (Class I to Class III), diastemas, macroglossia, prognathism.
Thyroid and parathyroid surgery: the recurrent laryngeal nerve is found first; damage leaves a hoarse, raspy voice, usually permanent.
Hyperthyroid: weight loss, tachycardia, heat intolerance; increased epinephrine sensitivity, avoid excessive vasoconstrictor when uncontrolled; accelerated eruption in children.
Hypothyroid (seen far more often than hyper): fatigue, weight gain, bradycardia; delayed eruption, macroglossia, delayed wound healing.

Thyroid storm (thyroid crisis, thyrotoxic crisis): rare; large hormone release in a short time; high fever, heart rate 140 or higher, agitation, shakiness, nausea, delirium, hypertension. Life-threatening: call 911.
PTH = fast acting: osteoclasts (resorption), kidney calcium reabsorption, calcitriol so the gut absorbs calcium. Vitamin D = long-term, activated in the kidney.
Calcitonin comes from the thyroid when calcium rises and reverses PTH's effects on bone cells.
Hyperparathyroidism in the mouth: loss of lamina dura (the white line of socket bone the PDL attaches to), radiolucent brown tumors (refer to the physician), tooth mobility.
Hypoparathyroidism: hypocalcemia, neuromuscular irritability, tetany.
Cortex: cortisol (stress, immunity, glucose) and aldosterone (sodium retention, potassium). Medulla: epinephrine and norepinephrine (vasoconstrictors, stress management).
Addison: hypotension, fatigue, hyperpigmentation; diffuse oral melanosis because high ACTH stimulates melanocytes.

Adrenal crisis triggers: long or stressful surgery, significant infection or trauma, missed steroid medication; after a big procedure, extra corticosteroid, dose set with the physician. Signs: severe hypotension, weakness, confusion, loss of consciousness, shock.
Cushing: moon face, buffalo hump, hyperglycemia; increased infection risk and delayed healing.
Alpha cells: glucagon (glycogen breakdown, gluconeogenesis). Beta cells: insulin (glucose into cells, storage).

Type 1 = autoimmune beta-cell destruction (insulin to survive). Type 2 = insulin resistance with hyperinsulinemia: insulin ineffective, not deficient. HbA1c: about 5 normal, below 7 well controlled, above 7 poorly controlled (implant failure, periodontal disease).
Diabetes in the mouth: xerostomia, candidiasis, burning mouth syndrome, delayed healing, more periodontal disease and caries. The perio link is bidirectional.
Poor diabetic healing: decreased neutrophil function, poor blood supply, impaired collagen synthesis.

Diabetic visit: review control and HbA1c, confirm meal and medication (metformin plus no breakfast: watch for a low), morning appointment. Hypoglycemia (sweating, tremors, confusion, tachycardia): finger-stick (a CGM may stop at its floor), under 60 give straight glucose, not table sugar; slow on a GLP-1 drug; IV dextrose or glucagon IM/subQ if it fails; unconscious, emergency protocols.
Puberty: gingival inflammation. Pregnancy: pregnancy gingivitis, pyogenic granuloma. Menopause: xerostomia, altered taste, osteoporosis.
Pack-years = packs per day times years smoked (1 pack a day for 40 years = 40).
preg: Progesterone from the corpus luteum prepares the endometrium for implantation (wider vessels, glycogen vacuoles). Without hCG the corpus luteum regresses into the corpus albicans about 14 days after ovulation.
About 250 million sperm deposited, about 50 reach the distal fallopian tube; sperm keep fertilizing capacity for 24 to 48 hours.
Estrogen at ovulation helps sperm: buffers the vaginal pH, thins the cervical mucus, increases myometrial contraction.
Three layers, outside in: expanded cumulus (he called it the corona radiata), zona pellucida, plasma membrane (oolemma).

ZP3 binding sets off the acrosomal reaction (hyaluronidases and proteases digest the zona). Then the sperm binds ZP2: the second meiotic division (the first was at ovulation) and the cortical (zonal) reaction, which blocks polyspermy. The pronuclei fuse into a zygote.
Capacitation: ejaculated sperm can't fertilize yet. In the female tract cholesterol leaves the membrane, blocking proteins go, calcium can enter, and the tail goes from wave-like to whip-like.
Fertilization usually happens in the distal fallopian tube; the fimbriae capture the oocyte, and cilia and peristalsis move it.
Estrogen constricts the opening of the uterus, holding the embryo back; progesterone relaxes the myometrium and lets the blastocyst in. Estrogen contracts, progesterone relaxes.
After ovulation: fertilization within 24 hours; blastocyst in the uterine cavity about day 4; implantation day 5 to 7; hCG from the trophoblasts about day 8.
Implantation at the blastocyst stage; its outer layer is the trophoblasts. The blastocyst secretes adhesion molecules, proteases and hCG.
Cytotrophoblasts = nurse cells. Syncytiotrophoblasts = invasion (proteases) and hormones (hCG, hPL).
Decidualization: more vessels, more glycogen, local immune suppression; with progesterone, endometrial cells become decidual cells.
hCG rescues the corpus luteum, which makes more progesterone and estrogen; LH and FSH stay suppressed. Pregnancy tests detect it (10 to 11 days after fertilization); it peaks at about 10 weeks.
hCG weakly stimulates the TSH receptor (transient gestational hyperthyroidism); estrogen raises TBG, so total T3 and T4 rise more than free.
The corpus luteum makes most progesterone and estrogen in the first trimester; the placenta, fully developed by its end, takes over.
Placenta: exchange, hormones (hCG, progesterone, estrogen, hPL), immune protection (maternal antibodies cross), waste into the mother's blood. Some drugs and viruses cross.
hPL (human chorionic somatomammotropin): breast growth; anti-insulin (lipolysis, fuel breakdown). Pregnancy is insulin resistant and hyperinsulinemic: gestational diabetes, multifactorial.
Relaxin (corpus luteum under hCG, and placenta): quiets the myometrium, relaxes pelvic ligaments, softens the cervix.

Estriol is pregnancy's estrogen (estradiol = cycle, estrone = menopause). The placenta has cholesterol desmolase and aromatase but lacks 17,20 desmolase: the fetal adrenal makes DHEA sulfate, the fetal liver 16-hydroxylates it, the placenta makes estriol. Estriol reflects fetal health. Progesterone the placenta makes alone.

Parturition about 40 weeks after the onset of the last menstrual period: uterine distention, more PGF2 alpha and oxytocin receptors, a rising estrogen-to-progesterone ratio, prostaglandins (more calcium; PGE2 softens the cervix), oxytocin from the posterior pituitary (synergizes with prostaglandins; positive feedback). After delivery oxytocin limits bleeding.
Breast in pregnancy: estrogen = ducts, branching, fat; progesterone = more alveoli; prolactin and cortisol = milk enzymes. Progesterone antagonizes prolactin, so full milk waits for delivery.
After delivery: prolactin = milk production; oxytocin = milk letdown (myoepithelial cells contract).

Dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin. Suckling lowers dopamine (prolactin rises, helped by prolactin releasing factor) and raises oxytocin (made in the hypothalamus, released from the posterior pituitary). Prolactin inhibits GnRH: amenorrhea.

Contraception: the pill's estrogen blunts the LH surge (it also thins the lining, and progestin thickens mucus); high-dose estrogen, the IUD and progesterone receptor antagonists prevent implantation; barriers, abstinence and withdrawal prevent contact.
sexster: His Case 1: avoid testosterone in BPH, in pregnancy (absolute) and in a man with breast cancer; avoid estrogen in breast cancer and after any thromboembolism.

DHEA (dehydroepiandrosterone, prasterone) is the testosterone precursor sold over the counter; every other testosterone product is Schedule III. (The slide's table mislabels DHEA as dihydrotestosterone.)
5-alpha-reductase reduces testosterone to DHT, the active form; aromatase turns testosterone into estradiol.
DHT stimulates growth; estradiol closes the epiphyses. No aromatase: very tall, osteoporotic bones; treat with estradiol.
Testosterone: more red cells (refractory anemia), water and electrolyte retention (poor in hypertension), lower HDL, more muscle; lower plasma CBG, TBG, SHBG and transferrin.
Sex steroids are lipophilic, ride on SHBG, bind nuclear receptors and change gene expression, so their effects take time.
Know testosterone and testosterone cypionate (Depo-Testosterone), the IM depot; testosterone and its injectable forms are 1 to 1 androgenic to anabolic.
Androgen uses: male hypogonadism, breast tumors, anabolic effects, refractory anemia, osteoporosis, growth, andropause.

Androgen side effects are worse in women and children. Women: hirsutism, deep voice, enlarged clitoris, smaller breasts (can be permanent). Men: sleep apnea, priapism, gynecomastia (from conversion to estradiol).
Most important testosterone side effect: hepatotoxicity (screen; no testosterone with liver disease). Apply the gel at bedtime so it isn't passed to a child.

GnRH analogs (goserelin, Zoladex; leuprolide): continuous stimulation switches off FSH and LH, so testosterone falls. Prostate cancer, BPH, precocious puberty, chemical castration. Impotence, gynecomastia.
5-alpha-reductase inhibitors: finasteride (Proscar, higher strength, for BPH; Propecia, lower strength, for alopecia) and dutasteride (Avodart). Gynecomastia, sexual dysfunction.
Androgen receptor antagonists: flutamide (Eulexin), bicalutamide (Casodex). Prostate cancer; excess androgens in women. GI upset (least with bicalutamide), gynecomastia, hepatotoxicity.
Natural estrogens: estradiol (ovary); estrone and estriol (liver and peripheral tissues), which recirculate through bile and gut. Oral estrogen has more liver effects.
Estrogen raises clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and lowers antithrombin III; raises HDL and triglycerides; opposes PTH-driven bone resorption; maintains skin.
Estradiol (patch, gel, injection); ethinyl estradiol in oral contraceptives; estrone, the main ingredient of Premarin, for menopause.
Estrogen side effects: nausea, fluid retention, breakthrough bleeding, breast tenderness; clots, endometrial and breast cancer, hypertension. Oral anticoagulants work less well.
Estrogen contraindications: pregnancy, incomplete bone growth, undiagnosed genital bleeding, any clot or stroke (even 10 years ago), heart disease, family history of breast or uterine cancer.
SERMs are tissue-selective because ER-alpha and ER-beta are expressed at different levels in different tissues.
Tamoxifen (Nolvadex): breast antagonist, uterine agonist (uterine cancer, clots); only for ER-positive breast cancer.
Raloxifene (Evista): postmenopausal osteoporosis; no endometrial or breast stimulation; DVT and PE risk 2 to 3 times higher (his dental case: clots during immobilization).
Clomiphene (Clomid): blocks estrogen's negative feedback, so the LH and FSH pulses grow and ovulation follows; multiple births, ovarian cysts.
Aromatase inhibitors (anastrozole, Arimidex): block testosterone to estradiol, for breast cancer; hot flashes and thromboembolism; not with liver damage or before menopause.
Progestins activate the progestin receptor and suppress FSH, preventing ovulation; hypertension, lower HDL. Progestin-only pills when estrogen is ruled out; levonorgestrel is the common one.
Plan B (levonorgestrel): within 72 hours, no prescription. Ulipristal (Ella, an antagonist): up to 120 hours, prescription. Mifepristone also blocks glucocorticoid receptors: not in Addison disease.
hemeintro: Blood cells: red cells are most of them (about 99 percent) and carry oxygen and carbon dioxide; platelets are megakaryocyte pieces from the bone marrow that start clotting ("just knowledge you should know").

White cells: two classes, five types. Granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) and agranulocytes (monocytes, lymphocytes). Most to least common: neutrophils 50 to 70 percent, lymphocytes 30 to 40, monocytes 2 to 8, eosinophils 1 to 4, basophils under 1 (Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas).
Hematopoiesis: one pluripotential stem cell; the lymphoid line makes B and T cells, the myeloid line stays in the marrow and makes red cells, megakaryocytes, granulocytes and monocytes.

Innate: what the body just does (skin and mucosa, low pH, lysozyme, thiocyanate in saliva, interferons, phagocytes, NK cells). Adaptive: after a first contact with an antigen, with memory; humoral means B cells and antibodies, cellular means T cells.
Neutrophil: multi-lobed nucleus, primary granules with elastase and myeloperoxidase, glycogen; about 10 hours in the blood; the first line of defense against bacteria.

Eosinophil: bilobed nucleus, red granules (peroxidase, major basic protein); parasites and hay fever; IgE receptors. Basophil: under 1 percent, dark blue to purple granules (heparin, histamine); IgE receptors; asthma.
Monocyte: one nucleus, not lobed; about 3 days in the blood, then the tissue macrophage; MHC II. Lymphocyte: a big nucleus in a thin rim of cytoplasm; NK cells large, B and T cells small.
B cell: surface IgM and IgD; when its antibody fits, it recruits helper T cells and becomes a plasma cell that releases that antibody, in a secondary organ.
Helper T: CD4, antigen on MHC II from antigen-presenting cells; helps the B cells. Cytotoxic T: CD8, MHC I; kills what it binds. T cells carry memory.

NK cell: no B or T markers, no specific receptor. MHC class I on a healthy cell binds its inhibitory receptor: no killing. Missing MHC class I: killed. Far more activating ligands: induced killing. CD16 binds IgG in ADCC.

Primary organs: just the bone marrow (B cells) and the thymus (T cells), not GALT; they make B and T cells immunocompetent without antigen. Everything else (lymph nodes, MALT and GALT, spleen) is secondary.
Stroma: reticular cells and type III collagen in every lymphoid organ except the thymus, whose stroma is epithelioreticular cells.

Thymus: behind the manubrium; very large in babies, fat by the teens; 95 to 99 percent of thymocytes selected out. Cortex dense and dark, medulla lighter (Hassall's corpuscles). Blood-thymus barrier: epithelioreticular cells, perivascular connective tissue, capillary wall.
T cell education: in through postcapillary venules, out to the cortex, positive then negative selection, leave CD4 or CD8 positive for the secondary organs.

Lymph node route: afferent lymphatic, subcapsular sinus, trabecular sinuses, efferent lymphatic. Initial T and B activation in the paracortex, B activation in a primary follicle, B cells multiply in the germinal center, plasma cells secrete antibody in the medulla.

Lymph node cells: B cells in the cortex's follicles, T cells in the paracortex; dendritic cells present to T cells; follicular dendritic cells sit among germinal center B cells and lack MHC II; blood lymphocytes enter by high endothelial venules.
MALT: Peyer's patches in the ileum, under M cells that take microbes from the lumen; IgA into the lumen.

Tonsils: pharyngeal (back of the nasal cavity), tubal (at the auditory tube's opening), palatine (back of the throat, with crypts that trap material), lingual (back of the tongue). A child's inflamed pharyngeal tonsil is adenoiditis.

Spleen: the splenic artery, off the celiac trunk, brings blood-borne antigens in at the hilum; no afferent lymphatics; white pulp and red pulp; filters blood, removes old red cells and platelets, stores a third of the platelets.
White pulp: the PALS, T cells around the central artery (PALS means spleen), B cell nodules, and the marginal zone. Red pulp, most of the spleen: cords and sinusoids.

Splenic sinuses: rod-shaped, loosely packed endothelial cells, macrophage processes, strands of basal lamina at right angles, no smooth muscle, no pericytes. In the open circulation, blood squeezes from the cords back into the sinuses.
lymleuk: He said: don't freak out; know the basics. The categories (B or T, indolent or aggressive, acute or chronic, myeloid or lymphoid) and the underlined molecular associations; not the CD markers or the flow cytometry details.

Lymphoma: a cancer of lymphocytes, in nodes, spleen or lymphoid tissue anywhere; the tissue makes the diagnosis (he prefers the whole node excised). For flow cytometry, send it fresh, not in formalin.
B symptoms, his high-yield clues: a fever of 38 °C or higher, drenching night sweats, weight loss of at least 10% of body weight in 6 months. Tuberculosis can cause them too, so sample the tissue.
Benign node: rubbery, well circumscribed, follicles in the cortex, open sinuses. Lymphoma: fleshy, plump, architecture effaced by a monotonous population.

Flow cytometry reads surface antigens: B, T or myeloid; mature or blast; something abnormal. Kappa only or lambda only (normal about 3 to 1) means a clone. Forward scatter = size, side scatter = granularity.
Lymphomas resemble their normal counterpart: germinal center = follicular, mantle zone = mantle cell, marginal zone = marginal zone lymphoma. 85 to 90% of lymphoid neoplasms are B-cell.

Hodgkin: usually localized, central nodes, contiguous spread, extranodal uncommon, blood never involved, few bizarre cells; ABVD. Non-Hodgkin: usually widespread, peripheral nodes, can skip, often extranodal, blood can be involved; often CHOP.
Staging: one site or several, above or below the diaphragm or both, extranodal sites, or disseminated; disseminated is stage 4, the most aggressive.

Leukemia: neoplastic cells replace the marrow and blood; it starts in the marrow and spreads to spleen, liver and nodes; fatal untreated. Marrow failure (anemia, bleeding, infection) plus bone pain, organomegaly and gingival hypertrophy.
Neutrophil line: myeloblast, promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band, PMN. Blasts in the blood are abnormal except in newborns.
Marrow sampling: posterior iliac crest (core and aspirate) in adults; tibia in small children and the sternum (heart below), aspirate only.

Acute: blasts over 20%, rapid onset, under 6 months untreated, severely low platelets. Chronic myeloid: under 20% blasts, insidious, 2 to 6 years, high white count, milder cytopenias, organomegaly. Both die of infection or bleeding.

AML: any blast count with a defining genetic abnormality, otherwise over 20%; adults (median 65); medium to large blasts, Auer rods. ALL: children (usually 1 to 5, poor prognosis under 1); small blasts, scant cytoplasm, no granules, never Auer rods.

CLL/SLL: one disease of small mature B cells (blood = CLL, node = SLL), over 70, soccer-ball chromatin and smudge cells; CLL at least 5 × 10⁹/L, below that monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis; infections; largely incurable.

Indolent B-cell: CLL/SLL, follicular, mantle cell, marginal zone. Aggressive B-cell: DLBCL, Burkitt. T-cell: peripheral T-cell (aggressive), mycosis fungoides (indolent), Sézary (aggressive), extranodal NK/T.
Follicular: back-to-back follicles, t(14;18) keeps BCL2 on so cells don't die; widespread but often asymptomatic; median survival over 17 years.
Mantle cell: mantle zone, t(11;14) (nothing else has it), cyclin D1 stain means mantle cell; older patients; survival much improved.

Marginal zone (MALT), the one you'll see most: stomach with H. pylori, ocular adnexa with Chlamydia psittaci, salivary gland with Sjögren, thyroid with Hashimoto; lymphoepithelial lesions; very good prognosis.
DLBCL: about 30%; large cells (over twice a small lymphocyte), diffuse; grows fast, more B symptoms; de novo or transformed; R-CHOP.
Burkitt: very aggressive, t(8;14) MYC with IGH, starry sky (the key finding), the jaw in endemic Burkitt, EBV; 90% of children and 80% of adults survive.

Classic Hodgkin: recognize the Reed-Sternberg cells (very large, prominent nucleoli, few among reactive cells); nodular sclerosis has fibrous bands; EBV; over 80% cured. Subtype differences not needed.
Plasma cell neoplasms: solitary (rib, spine) or multifocal myeloma in the marrow; rouleaux, M-spike, lytic bone, high calcium, kidney damage, anemia (CRAB).

Peripheral T-cell: very aggressive, B symptoms, poor response to chemotherapy. Mycosis fungoides: most common skin lymphoma, indolent. Sézary: erythroderma, nodes, cerebriform cells in the blood; aggressive. Extranodal NK/T: EBV, necrosis, perforated palate.
CML, the chronic leukemia to know: t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome, BCR-ABL1 kinase always on; very high count with every stage of maturation; hypercellular marrow; imatinib blocks the kinase.
APL: t(15;17) PML-RARA, maturation stops at the promyelocyte, numerous Auer rods; DIC (clotting and bleeding at once) can kill; all-trans retinoic acid with arsenic trioxide cures most.
Acute monocytic leukemia: it can show in the mouth, gums swollen with leukemic cells (myeloid sarcoma). Acute leukemia can arise de novo or from MDS or CML.
mpath: Study guide: cryptorchidism; the categories of testicular tumors (germ cell, seminoma); the infections of the male tract; BPH, prostatic adenocarcinoma and Gleason grading.

The urinary collecting system (renal pelvis, ureters, bladder, urethra) is lined by urothelium (once transitional epithelium), 5 to 7 layers with umbrella cells on top; the distal urethra is squamous.
Vesicoureteral reflux: repeated UTIs in children, ascending to the kidneys. Stones lodge where the ureter enters the bladder. A diverticulum can get infected and grow a carcinoma.
90% of urinary tract tumors are urothelial carcinomas, mostly in the bladder. Bladder cancer: 4th cancer in men, rare in women; minimal painless hematuria; expensive (lifelong surveillance).

Urothelial carcinoma risks: smoking (4 times, and quitting doesn't lower it), dyes, rubber, leather, pelvic radiation, cyclophosphamide, catheters. Schistosoma haematobium: squamous cell carcinoma (Egypt).
Bladder carcinoma: low grade = uniform nuclei, high grade = nuclear pleomorphism; the stage = how deep into the wall (muscularis propria, then the prostate).
Hypospadias: the urethra opens ventrally. Epispadias: dorsally. Phimosis: a foreskin that can't retract; smegma, inflammation, then penile carcinoma.
HPV 6 and 11: condyloma acuminatum, benign, verrucous. HPV 16 and 18: PeIN, flat and red, 30% invasive if untreated. HPV-independent PeIN: men over 60, lichen sclerosus.
Penile squamous cell carcinoma: rare in the US, poor hygiene and phimosis, indolent, spreads to the inguinal nodes.
Testis: tunica vaginalis (peritoneum) and tunica albuginea; Sertoli cells guide spermatogenesis inside the tubules; Leydig cells outside make testosterone. Both are sex cord-stromal cells.
Hydrocele: fluid in the tunica vaginalis. Epididymitis: gonorrhea, chlamydia, or a UTI. Orchitis: uncommon. Emergencies: torsion and inguinal hernia.
Cryptorchidism: body heat halts spermatogenesis; wait up to the second year, then surgery. Surgery prevents infertility; the testicular cancer risk stays.
Testicular tumors: 95% germ cell, cured in over 95%. Seminoma: most frequent, 30s-40s, white and solid, no marker, radiosensitive. Non-seminomatous: embryonal, yolk sac, choriocarcinoma, teratoma.
Prostate: BPH around the urethra (transition zone), obstructs, after 50. Carcinoma in the peripheral zone: most frequent cancer in men, PSA, osteoblastic bone metastases, Gleason grade.
fpath: Study guide: the vulva, vagina and cervix; neoplastic versus non-neoplastic; infections; HPV and cervical neoplasia; age patterns. Key terms: lichen sclerosus, condyloma acuminatum, sarcoma botryoides, HPV, infectious vaginitis.
Paramesonephric ducts fuse: uterus and upper third of the vagina (unfused: fallopian tubes). Lower vagina: urogenital sinus. Uterus: bladder in front, rectum behind.
Endocervix: mucinous glandular. Ectocervix: non-keratinizing squamous. The transformation zone, where they "fight": inflamed, open to HPV, where cervical cancer arises.
Squamous intraepithelial lesions: low grade can regress; high grade progresses. 90% HPV. Koilocyte: big nucleus, clear halo. High grade: high N:C ratio, pleomorphic nuclei.
Cervical cancer: 4th in women worldwide (breast 1st); less in the US thanks to Pap screening; the HPV vaccine works but takes decades; management is now risk-based.
Myometrium: stops each cycle's bleeding and expels the baby. Endometrium: straight "tubes in a rack" under estrogen, coiled and secreting under progesterone.
Chronic endometritis: plasma cells, infertility, antibiotics. Endometrial polyp: sample it all in older women.
Endometrial carcinoma: endometrioid (estrogen excess, obesity, less aggressive, younger) vs the other type (over 65, aggressive).
Leiomyoma: very common, well circumscribed, abnormal bleeding. Leiomyosarcoma: aggressive, to the lung. Ovary: mostly epithelial tumors; ovarian cancer is lethal.
Vagina: vaginitis is the most common problem. Candida: pseudohyphae. Trichomonas: sexually transmitted protozoan with prolongations. Atrophic vaginitis: older women, not infectious.
Sarcoma botryoides (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma): girls under 5, good prognosis if treated in time. Vaginal squamous cell carcinoma: reproductive years.
Vulva: lichen simplex chronicus (thick, leathery, scratching); lichen sclerosus (atrophic, parchment, carcinoma risk); lichen planus (with oral lesions; fresh biopsy, immunofluorescence, steroids).
Condyloma acuminatum: HPV 6 and 11, benign. Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma: HPV 16 and 18 (radiosensitive), or lichen sclerosus in women over 60.
Breast: a modified skin gland along the milk line (axilla to groin). Mastitis (antibiotics), duct ectasia (nipple retraction), fat necrosis (seatbelt).
DCIS: treat (surgery ± radiotherapy). LCIS: benign (WHO). Invasive ductal: glands; lobular: single files. Paget: scaly red nipple, look for the carcinoma. ER, PR, HER2 guide drugs.
Male breast: same diseases, cancer found late (no screening). Gynecomastia: obese men (aromatase), weightlifters on testosterone.
