items.h: Hormonal support of pregnancy and the role of the placenta/corpus luteum
items.body:
Without a pregnancy the corpus luteum dies about 14 days after ovulation and its hormones crash. In a pregnancy, hCG from the embryo rescues it: the corpus luteum carries the first trimester, then the placenta takes over the hormones, with the fetus's help for estrogen.

Know this
  • Progesterone from the corpus luteum is the key hormone that prepares the endometrium for implantation (wider vessels, glycogen vacuoles). With no pregnancy, about 14 days after ovulation the corpus luteum regresses into the corpus albicans and estrogen and progesterone fall abruptly.
  • hCG is made by the trophoblasts (the syncytiotrophoblasts), later the placenta, from about 8 days after ovulation. The corpus luteum doesn't make it; it responds to it.
  • hCG rescues the corpus luteum: no regression, and more progesterone and estrogen. LH and FSH stay suppressed, so the cycle and periods stop. The lecture's summary: "hCG prevents the regression of corpus luteum, slows production of LH and FSH."
  • A pregnancy test measures hCG: in urine or blood about 10 to 11 days after fertilization. It peaks at about 10 weeks, toward the end of the first trimester, then declines.
  • hCG weakly stimulates the TSH receptor: a transient gestational hyperthyroidism. Estrogen raises TBG, so total T3 and T4 can double while free T3 and T4 barely rise.
  • First trimester: the corpus luteum makes most of the progesterone and estrogen. The placenta starts developing shortly after implantation, is fully developed by the end of the first trimester, then takes over hormone production.
  • The placenta exchanges gases and nutrients (oxygen, water, electrolytes and nutrients in; carbon dioxide and waste out, into the mother's blood), makes hormones, and protects the fetus while letting maternal antibodies through. It is not an absolute barrier: some drugs and viruses cross.
  • The steroids start from the mother's cholesterol. The placenta makes progesterone on its own, but it lacks 17,20 desmolase, so estrogen needs the fetus: the fetal adrenal makes DHEA sulfate, the fetal liver 16-hydroxylates it, and the placenta's aromatase makes estriol.
  • Estriol is the estrogen of pregnancy (estradiol is the cycle's, estrone menopause's). Because it needs a working fetal adrenal and liver, the mother's estriol reflects the health of the fetus.
  • Human placental lactogen (hPL), also called human chorionic somatomammotropin, from the syncytiotrophoblasts: breast growth, and anti-insulin actions (lipolysis, breakdown of carbohydrates and proteins) that keep fuel flowing to the fetus. So pregnancy is insulin resistant and hyperinsulinemic, and some mothers get gestational diabetes, which the lecture called multifactorial.
  • Relaxin, from the corpus luteum (under hCG) and the placenta, inhibits myometrial contractions ("the last thing we want is a preterm delivery"), relaxes the pelvic ligaments and softens the cervix.
HormoneMade byMain job
hCGTrophoblasts, then the placentaRescues the corpus luteum; the pregnancy test
ProgesteroneCorpus luteum, then the placenta on its ownReadies the endometrium; relaxes the myometrium
EstriolPlacenta, with the fetal adrenal and liverPregnancy's estrogen; reflects fetal health
hPLSyncytiotrophoblasts (placenta)Breast growth; opposes insulin
RelaxinCorpus luteum and placentaKeeps the uterus quiet; softens the cervix

Watch for: hCG is made by the trophoblasts and acts on the corpus luteum; it doesn't turn it into the corpus albicans. Don't flip the steroids: progesterone alone, estrogen with the fetus, and the 16-hydroxylation is the fetal liver, not the kidney. The placenta isn't complete at implantation. hPL is not hCG, and it isn't made by the cytotrophoblasts (the nurse cells). Insulin rises in pregnancy. Relaxin quiets the uterus. The placenta doesn't make oxytocin. The lecture credits hCG itself with lowering LH and FSH; textbooks credit the high estrogen and progesterone it keeps up. No question depends on which.

items.h: Hormonal changes associated with delivery and the postpartum period
items.body:
Labor starts when stretch and a shift in hormones turn a quiet uterus into a contracting one. Oxytocin is "the big one," and it keeps working after the birth to limit bleeding; delivering the placenta drops progesterone, which lets milk production start.

Know this
  • Parturition comes about 40 weeks after the onset of the last menstrual period, not 40 weeks after fertilization.
  • Distention of the uterus by the growing fetus is a trigger: the stretch sets off the hormonal signals.
  • The uterus upregulates its receptors for PGF2 alpha and oxytocin.
  • The uterus becomes more sensitive to estrogen and less to progesterone: the estrogen-to-progesterone ratio rises and the myometrium shifts to contracting. Estrogen contracts, progesterone relaxes.
  • Uterine prostaglandins rise and raise intracellular calcium, so contractions get stronger. PGF2 alpha: contraction. PGE2: softens and thins the cervix.
  • Oxytocin from the mother's posterior pituitary (made in the hypothalamus) is "the big one": it drives the contractions and synergizes with the prostaglandins, by positive feedback (contractions bring more oxytocin).
  • Relaxin may help relax and thin the cervix at term.
  • After delivery, oxytocin keeps the uterus contracting once the placenta is out, which prevents excessive bleeding: "oxytocin has a role both during active delivery and post-delivery."
  • Delivering the placenta makes progesterone fall, which takes the brake off prolactin: full milk production begins.
  • Postpartum, suckling keeps prolactin high and releases oxytocin for letdown, and the high prolactin inhibits GnRH, so periods often stay away while breastfeeding.
SignalRole at delivery
Uterine stretchTrigger for the hormonal signals
Rising estrogen-to-progesterone ratioMyometrium shifts to contracting
PGF2 alphaContraction (its receptors go up)
PGE2Softens and thins the cervix
Oxytocin (posterior pituitary)Contractions, positive feedback; limits bleeding after delivery
Progesterone falls (placenta out)Frees prolactin to make milk

Watch for: "40 weeks after fertilization" is false: the count starts at the last menstrual period, about two weeks earlier. The PGF2 alpha and oxytocin receptors go up, not down. The ratio rises toward estrogen, which favors contraction. Don't swap the prostaglandins: PGE2 is the cervix, PGF2 alpha the contraction. After delivery oxytocin limits bleeding; it doesn't raise progesterone or rescue the corpus luteum.

items.h: Prolactin vs. oxytocin
items.body:
Two pituitary hormones with two jobs in the breast: "Prolactin sets the stage and creates all the milk products. Oxytocin is going to stimulate milk letdown." Prolactin makes the milk; oxytocin squeezes it out.

Know this
  • Prolactin = milk production. Oxytocin = milk letdown (ejection). A choice that swaps them is the obvious trap.
  • Prolactin comes from the anterior pituitary and is tonically inhibited by dopamine from the hypothalamus.
  • Oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary into the blood.
  • Prolactin, with cortisol, raises the milk enzymes during pregnancy, and after delivery it drives full milk production in the alveoli.
  • Oxytocin contracts the myoepithelial cells around each alveolus, which squeezes the milk out. It doesn't make milk or milk enzymes.
  • During pregnancy prolactin rises, especially late, but is antagonized by progesterone, so full milk waits for delivery.
  • Prolactin also inhibits GnRH: LH, FSH and the sex steroids fall, and periods stop.
  • Oxytocin also drives labor contractions (positive feedback) and limits bleeding after delivery.
  • Suckling turns both on: it lowers dopamine (so prolactin rises) and releases oxytocin.
ProlactinOxytocin
SourceAnterior pituitaryHypothalamus; released from the posterior pituitary
ControlDopamine holds it down; suckling lowers dopamineSuckling releases it
In the breastMilk enzymes and milk productionMyoepithelial cells contract: letdown
Pregnancy and laborRises, but progesterone antagonizes itLabor contractions, positive feedback
After deliveryFull milk; inhibits GnRHLetdown; limits uterine bleeding

Watch for: Oxytocin lets milk down by contracting the myoepithelial cells, not by making the alveolar cells produce milk enzymes. The brake on prolactin is dopamine, not oxytocin or GnRH. Progesterone doesn't make milk. Oxytocin comes from the posterior pituitary, not the anterior pituitary or the placenta.

items.h: Neuroendocrine effects of suckling
items.body:
Suckling is a reflex from the nipple to the hypothalamus. It takes the dopamine brake off prolactin and releases oxytocin, so one stimulus both makes the milk and lets it down, and the high prolactin also shuts the cycle down. On this slide Dr. Madison said: "mainly focus on this side of things. Dopamine being important."

Know this
  • At baseline the hypothalamus releases dopamine all the time, "a potent inhibitor of prolactin release from the anterior pituitary." Without a baby to feed, prolactin stays low.
  • Suckling decreases dopamine. The lecture adds that the baby's sounds and sight and the emotions of delivery can lower it too.
  • With dopamine down, the anterior pituitary releases prolactin, and prolactin releasing factor pushes it higher. Low dopamine means high prolactin.
  • Prolactin drives full milk production in the alveoli.
  • Suckling also makes the hypothalamus produce oxytocin, which is released from the posterior pituitary into the blood.
  • Oxytocin contracts the myoepithelial cells: milk letdown.
  • "One thing that I want to highlight": prolactin inhibits GnRH. Less GnRH means less LH and FSH and lower sex steroids, so amenorrhea. That is why a breastfeeding mother's periods often stop, the same mechanism as hyperprolactinemia from any cause.
  • This circuit turns on after delivery. Some prolactin is made in pregnancy, but progesterone holds it back.

Watch for: Suckling lowers dopamine: a statement that it raises dopamine, or a choice blaming "high dopamine from suckling," is wrong. Prolactin, not oxytocin, inhibits GnRH. A breastfeeding mother's missing periods are not leftover hCG keeping her corpus luteum alive. The lecture says the baby's sounds and sight lower dopamine; physiology texts tie the baby's cry mainly to oxytocin and letdown. No question depends on which.

items.h: Regulation of milk production and milk ejection
items.body:
The breast is built during pregnancy but kept from full milk production until delivery, because progesterone blocks prolactin. After delivery, making milk is prolactin's job and ejecting it is oxytocin's, and suckling keeps both going.

Know this
  • The high estrogen and progesterone of pregnancy (corpus luteum, then placenta) build the breast.
  • Estrogen: ductal and lobular growth and ductal branching, and more fat. Breast fat expresses aromatase, so the breast makes estrogen locally.
  • Progesterone: increases the number of alveoli, the milk-producing structures.
  • Prolactin (rising, especially late) and cortisol: both increase the milk enzymes. Human placental lactogen also helps breast tissue grow.
  • "What you should know": progesterone antagonizes prolactin, especially locally in the breast, so there may be a little milk but no full milk production until after delivery.
  • Delivering the placenta makes progesterone fall; the brake comes off, and prolactin drives full milk production in the alveoli.
  • Production stays on because suckling keeps dopamine low, so prolactin stays high, with prolactin releasing factor adding to it.
  • Ejection (letdown): suckling releases oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, which contracts the myoepithelial cells around each alveolus and squeezes the milk out.
HormoneDuring pregnancyAfter delivery
EstrogenDucts, branching, fatNot on the slide
ProgesteroneMore alveoli; antagonizes prolactinFalls when the placenta is delivered
Prolactin (with cortisol)Raises the milk enzymes, but held backFull milk production
OxytocinLabor contractionsMilk letdown
DopamineTonically inhibits prolactinSuckling lowers it

Watch for: Progesterone, not estrogen or prolactin, adds the alveoli; estrogen, not progesterone, grows and branches the ducts. Cortisol raises the milk enzymes, it doesn't lower them. Full milk waits for delivery because placental progesterone antagonizes prolactin, not because the alveoli are missing, the placenta makes dopamine, or oxytocin blocks prolactin. The lecture and slide name only progesterone as prolactin's antagonist in pregnancy (textbooks add estrogen); the hub's questions use progesterone.

terms.d: Human chorionic gonadotropin, made by the trophoblasts from about 8 days after ovulation. It rescues the corpus luteum, so progesterone and estrogen stay high and LH and FSH stay low, and it is what a pregnancy test measures (10 to 11 days after fertilization; peak at about 10 weeks).

The hormone that prepares the endometrium for implantation and relaxes the myometrium; made by the corpus luteum through the first trimester, then by the placenta on its own. In the breast it adds alveoli and antagonizes prolactin until it falls at delivery.
The anterior pituitary hormone of milk production, tonically inhibited by dopamine and released when suckling lowers dopamine. High prolactin inhibits GnRH, causing the amenorrhea of breastfeeding.

Made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary: it contracts the myoepithelial cells for milk letdown, drives labor contractions by positive feedback, and keeps the uterus contracting after delivery to limit bleeding. Not a placental hormone.

items.h: Major actions of estrogens, progestins, and androgens
items.body:
The sex steroids come from cholesterol, ride on SHBG and act on nuclear receptors, so their effects take time. Testosterone acts mostly as DHT or becomes estradiol; estrogen builds the female body, the uterine lining and bone, and raises clotting; progesterone matures the endometrium.

Know this
  • Synthesis: cholesterol, in several steps, to DHEA (dehydroepiandrosterone), then androstenedione, then testosterone.
  • Testosterone's two fates: 5-alpha-reductase reduces it to DHT, the active form ("Dihydrotestosterone is the active testosterone"), and aromatase turns it into estradiol.
  • How they act: lipophilic, carried on SHBG (the corticosteroids ride CBG); only the free hormone enters the cell, binds its nuclear receptor (DHT is the main androgen receptor ligand), and the complex changes gene expression, so the effect takes time.
  • Testosterone's effects: male differentiation and puberty; sperm formation; more red blood cells; retention of water and electrolytes; lower HDL; more protein synthesis and muscle; thicker skin; libido; and it lowers plasma CBG, TBG, SHBG and transferrin.
  • Growth: DHT stimulates growth and estradiol closes the epiphyses. A man without aromatase makes no estradiol and grows very tall with weak, osteoporotic bones; the treatment is estradiol.
  • The natural estrogens: estradiol (E2) from the ovary; estrone (E1) and estriol (E3) from the liver and peripheral tissues, which go out in the bile and are reabsorbed from the gut (enterohepatic recirculation).
  • Oral estrogens act more on the liver, including a rise in clotting factors. In the blood estrogen rides SHBG and albumin, and the free hormone binds the estrogen receptor.
  • Estrogen's effects: female maturation (vagina, uterus, secondary sex traits); growth of the uterine muscle and lining; raises HDL and triglycerides; maintains the skin and blood vessels (some teens get the pill for bad skin); antagonizes PTH-driven bone resorption; raises clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and lowers antithrombin III.
  • Progesterone (adrenal cortex, corpus luteum, placenta, testes): the action he stressed is maturation of the endometrium. Progestin drugs activate its receptor and suppress FSH (next item).
TestosteroneEstrogen
HDLLowers itRaises it (and triglycerides)
GrowthDHT stimulates growthEstradiol closes the epiphyses
BloodMore red blood cellsMore clotting factors, less antithrombin III
FluidRetains water and electrolytesFluid retention

Watch for: DHEA is dehydroepiandrosterone, the precursor; his slide's table mislabels it "dihydrotestosterone," and he corrected it in class. Testosterone lowers the binding globulins and HDL, travels on SHBG (not CBG) and acts on a nuclear receptor (not a cell-surface one). A man without aromatase is tall, not short. Estrogen grows the uterine lining; it doesn't thin it. Two slides disagree on estrogen and LDL, so lean on HDL. The rest of his second estrogen-effects slide (ACTH, well-being, binding globulins, FSH and LH inhibition) he skipped: not needed.

items.h: How hormonal contraceptives prevent pregnancy
items.body:
Hormonal contraception mostly works by stopping ovulation: a progestin, often with ethinyl estradiol, holds down FSH and LH. Women who can't take estrogen use a progestin alone. Emergency contraception is a big dose of a progestin (Plan B) or a progestin receptor blocker (ulipristal).

Know this
  • Progestins activate the progestin receptor, which suppresses FSH (and LH and estradiol), so there is no ovulation.
  • The combined pill's estrogen is ethinyl estradiol, the semi-synthetic one. Levonorgestrel is the most common progestin in oral contraceptives.
  • Women who can't take estrogen (a history or family history of thromboembolism, or breast or uterine cancer) avoid pills with ethinyl estradiol and take a progestin-only pill.
  • His Case 3: of ethinyl estradiol, estradiol, levonorgestrel and estrone, the least estrogenic is levonorgestrel, a progestin.
  • Dr. Madison's version (L17): the pill's estrogen blunts the LH surge, so there is no normal ovulation; it also thins the lining, and its progestin thickens the cervical mucus so sperm can't get into the uterus. High-dose estrogen prevents implantation (the lining proliferates but misses progesterone's preparation), and so do the IUD and progesterone receptor antagonists.
  • Plan B is a high dose of levonorgestrel: within 72 hours, no prescription.
  • Ulipristal (Ella) is a progestin receptor antagonist: up to 120 hours (5 days), prescription only. Same indication as Plan B.
  • Mifepristone blocks the progestin and the glucocorticoid receptor, so it is contraindicated in Addison disease. Anti-progestins are avoided when pregnancy is wanted soon.
  • Progestin cautions: hypertension (an adverse effect and a contraindication), lower HDL, and pregnancy wanted in the near future.
Plan BUlipristal (Ella)
What it isHigh-dose levonorgestrel, a progestinProgestin receptor antagonist
WindowWithin 72 hoursUp to 120 hours (5 days)
PrescriptionNot neededNeeded

Watch for: Progestins activate the progestin receptor; blocking it is what the anti-progestins do (ulipristal, mifepristone). Plan B is levonorgestrel, not ethinyl estradiol, and not ulipristal at another strength. Its window is 72 hours, not 24. Progestins lower HDL. Thick cervical mucus is the progestin's doing. The pill's estrogen blunts the LH surge; it doesn't trigger an early one, raise prolactin or act like hCG. Dr. Madison skipped the methods that keep sperm and egg apart.

items.h: Major drug classes that alter reproductive hormone signaling
items.body:
"The names will suggest to you how they work": each class supplies a hormone, blocks its receptor, or stops it from being made, so know what the target enzyme or receptor does. Learn the drugs his slides highlight in red (the table's "drugs to know"): "Pay attention to those drugs that I highlight in the slides, and you should be fine."

Know this
  • Androgens: testosterone, the standard (Schedule III; gels, a patch, a nasal gel, injections), and testosterone cypionate (Depo-Testosterone), the intramuscular depot, injected about once a week or once a month. Both are 1 to 1 androgenic to anabolic.
  • DHEA (prasterone), the precursor, is sold over the counter, the one testosterone product that escapes Schedule III.
  • GnRH analogs: goserelin (Zoladex), also leuprolide (Lupron). Natural GnRH comes in pulses; a long-acting analog stimulates without a pause, the pituitary cells switch off, and FSH, LH and testosterone fall. Mainly prostate cancer; also BPH, precocious puberty and chemical castration. Side effects are anti-sex-hormonal: impotence and gynecomastia.
  • Estrogens: estradiol (patch, gel, injection) for replacement; ethinyl estradiol, semi-synthetic, for oral contraceptives; estrone, the main ingredient of Premarin (from pregnant mares), for menopause therapy.
  • SERMs are tissue-selective because ER-alpha and ER-beta are expressed at different levels in different tissues: an agonist in one, an antagonist in another.
  • Tamoxifen (Nolvadex): antagonist in the breast, agonist in the uterus; only for ER-positive breast cancer ("That is the only time you give tamoxifen").
  • Raloxifene (Evista): postmenopausal osteoporosis; no endometrial or breast stimulation. On his SERM table, uterine cell proliferation separates it from tamoxifen; both promote bone, and neither stimulates breast cells or inhibits ovulation.
  • Clomiphene (Clomid): a weak agonist, strong antagonist that blocks estrogen's negative feedback, so the LH and FSH pulses grow and the ovary ovulates; it needs an intact hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis.
  • "Tamoxifen for breast cancer, raloxifene for osteoporosis, Clomid... to stimulate ovulation."
  • Aromatase inhibitors: anastrozole (Arimidex), also letrozole and exemestane, block testosterone's conversion to estradiol, for breast cancer.
  • Progestins and anti-progestins are the item above; the 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors and androgen receptor antagonists the item below.

Watch for: Anastrozole blocks the enzyme; tamoxifen blocks the receptor. Goserelin doesn't block a receptor or 5-alpha-reductase, and it doesn't mimic the pulses: it works by never pausing. Osteoporosis is raloxifene's use, not a GnRH analog's or clomiphene's. Premarin is estrone, for menopause; ethinyl estradiol is the pill's. Cypionate is no more anabolic than testosterone. Said not needed: the other androgen analogs on his table and the rarely used SERMs (toremifene, ospemifene, bazedoxifene, fulvestrant).

items.h: Drugs that block androgen receptors or androgen metabolism
items.body:
"An anti-androgen either blocks testosterone at its receptor, prevents its activation to DHT, or shuts down its production." This item is the first two: the 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors stop testosterone from becoming DHT, and the androgen receptor antagonists compete with it at the receptor. The GnRH analogs, which shut down production, are in the item above.

Know this
  • Testosterone isn't very active until 5-alpha-reductase reduces it to DHT: its bioactivation. His Case 2: the enzyme that makes testosterone biologically active is 5-alpha-reductase (aromatase would make estradiol).
  • 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors: finasteride (Proscar, Propecia) and dutasteride (Avodart). They block testosterone's conversion to DHT.
  • Uses: BPH and alopecia. Proscar and Propecia are the same drug, finasteride: "the difference between Proscar and Propecia is the dose, the strength of the tablet," and the indication. Higher strength for BPH, lower strength for hair loss.
  • Side effects: gynecomastia and sexual dysfunction. His Case 4, in the dental chair: a man on finasteride for hair loss with a lower libido and breast tenderness; the drug is blocking 5-alpha-reductase.
  • Androgen receptor antagonists: flutamide (Eulexin) and bicalutamide (Casodex) (nilutamide and enzalutamide are on the slide too): competitive antagonism at the androgen receptor.
  • Uses: prostate cancer in men and excess androgens in women.
  • Side effects: GI disturbances (least with bicalutamide), gynecomastia and hepatotoxicity.
  • Gynecomastia is on all three anti-androgen lists.
GnRH analogs5-alpha-reductase inhibitorsAndrogen receptor antagonists
DrugsGoserelin, leuprolideFinasteride, dutasterideFlutamide, bicalutamide
HowSwitch off FSH and LHBlock testosterone to DHTCompete at the receptor
UsesProstate cancer, BPH, precocious puberty, chemical castrationBPH, alopeciaProstate cancer; excess androgens in women
Side effectsImpotence, gynecomastiaGynecomastia, sexual dysfunctionGI upset, gynecomastia, hepatotoxicity

Watch for: Finasteride blocks 5-alpha-reductase, not the androgen receptor or aromatase, and it does have hormonal side effects. Bicalutamide causes the least GI upset, not the most. The three classes don't all block the receptor. Match the pairs: finasteride and dutasteride (5-alpha-reductase); bicalutamide and enzalutamide (receptor); goserelin and leuprolide (GnRH); anastrozole and letrozole (aromatase). Dr. Fasinu wasn't sure of the tablet strengths in class: know which is higher.

items.h: Important therapeutic effects and adverse effects
items.body:
Each class has its uses and an adverse effect he kept coming back to: hepatotoxicity for testosterone, and thromboembolism for the estrogens, a clot risk the SERMs and aromatase inhibitors share. His opening case asks which hormone to avoid in which patient.

Know this
  • Case 1: avoid testosterone in BPH, pregnancy (he called it absolute) and a man with breast cancer; avoid estrogen in breast cancer and after any thromboembolism.
  • Androgen uses: male hypogonadism, some breast tumors in women, anabolic effects, refractory anemia, osteoporosis, growth, and andropause.
  • Testosterone's most important adverse effect is hepatotoxicity: patients are screened, and liver disease rules it out. Also avoid it in pregnancy, heart disease, and prostate or breast cancer in men.
  • Androgen side effects are worse in women and children. Women: hirsutism, a deepened voice, an enlarged clitoris, smaller breasts, sometimes irreversible. Men: sleep apnea, priapism, and gynecomastia, believed to come from testosterone converted to estradiol. Both: acne, edema, jaundice, lower HDL and higher LDL.
  • Testosterone gel or cream: apply it last thing at night, since a hug can pass it through the skin to a child.
  • Estrogen uses: primary hypogonadism, postmenopausal hormone therapy, oral contraceptives, suppressing ovulation in intractable dysmenorrhea or hirsutism, fertility treatment.
  • Thromboembolism is "the most serious and most common side effect of estrogens": they raise clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and lower antithrombin III.
  • Other estrogen side effects. Common: nausea, fluid retention, breakthrough bleeding, breast tenderness. Serious: clots, endometrial and breast cancer, hypertension.
  • Fluid retention is shared by androgens and estrogens and worsens hypertension and heart failure.
  • In menopause therapy, adding progesterone reduces or eliminates estrogen's added uterine cancer risk.
  • Estrogen contraindications: pregnancy, incomplete bone growth, undiagnosed genital bleeding, a stroke or any clot, even 10 years ago, heart disease, a family history of breast or uterine cancer.
  • Estrogens make oral anticoagulants such as warfarin work less well, because they raise clotting factor production.
  • SERMs share the clot risk: raloxifene raises DVT and PE risk 2 to 3 times; tamoxifen raises uterine cancer and clot risk. His Case 5: a woman on raloxifene after an extraction; watch for a clot while she is immobilized.
  • Clomiphene: multiple births and ovarian cysts.
  • Aromatase inhibitors: "at least" remember hot flashes and thromboembolism. Not with hepatic damage or before menopause.
  • Progestins: contraception, dysmenorrhea, endometriosis, precocious puberty; adverse effects hypertension, lower HDL, cancer risk with estrogen. The anti-androgens' side effects are in the item above.

EstrogensThromboembolismAny clot or stroke, breast cancer, pregnancy, heart disease
SERMsClots (raloxifene 2 to 3 times)A history of DVT or PE
Aromatase inhibitorsHot flashes, thromboembolismPremenopausal women, hepatic damage
ProgestinsHypertension, lower HDLHypertension, pregnancy wanted soon

Watch for: Androgens lower HDL. Gynecomastia on testosterone comes from estradiol, not DHT. Hirsutism is an androgen side effect, not an estrogen one; preventing DVT is not an estrogen use; BPH is a reason to avoid testosterone, not a use. Estrogen makes warfarin work less well. Raloxifene's dental risk is a clot, not gingival overgrowth, immunosuppression or low calcium. His slide's "thrombolytic complications" means clots forming. For pregnancy, Case 1's answer is testosterone (aloud he said estrogen is used in a few pregnant women; his slide lists pregnancy as an estrogen contraindication). For children the slide says extreme caution and aloud he was firmer; no question depends on it.

terms.d: Long-acting copies of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, chiefly goserelin (Zoladex) and leuprolide (Lupron). Natural GnRH is pulsed; the analogs stimulate continuously, so the pituitary switches off and FSH, LH and testosterone fall. Mainly for prostate cancer; side effects are impotence and gynecomastia.

Progesterone and its analogs (hydroxyprogesterone, levonorgestrel) that activate the progestin receptor and suppress FSH and LH, preventing ovulation: the progestin-only pill and Plan B (high-dose levonorgestrel, within 72 hours). Adverse effects: hypertension and lower HDL.

Drugs that lower androgen activity three ways: GnRH analogs shut down production, 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) stop activation to DHT, and androgen receptor antagonists (flutamide, bicalutamide) block the receptor. Gynecomastia is common to all three.

Finasteride (Proscar, higher strength, for BPH; Propecia, lower strength, for hair loss) and dutasteride (Avodart): they block testosterone's conversion to DHT, its active form. Side effects: gynecomastia and sexual dysfunction, like the low libido and breast tenderness of his dental case.

items.h: Recognition and major functions of RBCs, platelets, and leukocytes
items.body:
Blood holds three kinds of cells: red cells, platelets and white cells. Know each by its described features (there are no stained images on the exam) and by its job. For the white cells, "we've got two classes and 5 types."

Know this
  • Erythrocytes are most of the cells in the blood, about 99 percent, and carry oxygen and carbon dioxide.
  • Platelets are pieces of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow, and they initiate blood clotting: "just knowledge you should know."
  • Granulocytes, with prominent granules: neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils. Agranulocytes, without them: monocytes and lymphocytes (B, T and NK cells).
  • Most to least common: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils (Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas; the shares are in the table).
  • Lymphocyte sizes: NK cells are the large ones; B and T cells are smaller.
  • Hematopoiesis: one pluripotential stem cell, two lines. The lymphoid line makes the B and T lymphocytes. The myeloid line stays in the marrow and makes the red cells, megakaryocytes (platelets), granulocytes and monocytes.
  • In an adult, every blood cell comes from the bone marrow.

Watch for: Platelets are made in the bone marrow, not the spleen (the spleen stores about a third of them and clears the old ones). Red cells carry the gases and platelets clot, never the reverse. The monocyte comes from the myeloid line even though it has no prominent granules. Said not needed: the counts per liter in his table ("no reason to memorize the typical concentration of cells") and the colony-forming unit names.

items.h: Functions of neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, monocytes, and lymphocytes
items.body:
Each white cell has one main job, and the bank asks it from a description or a raised count: neutrophils for bacteria, eosinophils for parasites and allergy, basophils for histamine and asthma, monocytes for the macrophage they become.

Know this
  • Neutrophil: the main phagocyte of the blood and the first line of defense against bacteria; in the blood about 10 hours, then into the tissues. A multi-lobed nucleus, a lot of glycogen, primary granules with elastase and myeloperoxidase, and a second kind with lysozyme and proteases.
  • Eosinophil: peroxidase binds microorganisms and helps kill them; major basic protein (MBP) disrupts the membranes of parasites and makes basophils release histamine.
  • Eosinophils rise in parasitic infections (protozoa, helminths) and in allergic reactions such as hay fever, and carry IgE receptors.
  • Basophil: granules of heparin and vasoactive substances such as histamine, released when IgE binds its IgE receptors; a prominent role in bronchial asthma.
  • Monocyte: in the blood about 3 days, then into the tissues, where it becomes the macrophage (the mononuclear phagocytic system). It phagocytoses bacteria, cells and debris, and its MHC class II presents antigen to helper T cells.
  • Lymphocytes: immunocompetent cells that recognize and respond to antigen: B cells (become antibody-making plasma cells), T cells (help or kill) and NK cells (kill altered cells).

Watch for: About 10 hours is the neutrophil; about 3 days is the monocyte. Eosinophils and basophils share a bilobed nucleus and IgE receptors: the granules tell them apart. The monocyte becomes the macrophage, not the plasma cell (that's the B cell), a mast cell or a megakaryocyte. MBP attacks parasites; it is not an Fc receptor (that's the NK cell's CD16). He read the granule labels as his slide has them, "primary" and "azure"; histology texts call the primary ones azurophilic. Learn the contents: no question asks which kind is azurophilic.

items.h: Innate vs. adaptive immunity
items.body:
Innate immunity is what "your body just does": defenses already in place, aimed at nothing in particular. Adaptive immunity is built by B and T cells after a first contact with a specific antigen, and it often leaves memory. The two work together.

Know this
  • Innate (nonspecific): pre-existing defenses, ready before any contact with a microbe.
  • Its five parts: physical barriers (skin and mucous membranes); chemical defenses such as low pH; secretory substances: lysozyme, thiocyanate in saliva, interferons; phagocytes (macrophages, neutrophils, monocytes); and NK cells.
  • Adaptive (specific): acquired resistance. A first contact with a specific antigen starts reactions carried out by B and T cells, and it often leaves immune memory.
  • Humoral = B cells and antibodies, which mark invaders for destruction by other cells. Cellular = T cells, which target transformed and virus-infected cells.
  • His shortcut: "When you hear the word humoral, think B-cell response," and B cells mean antibody production.
InnateAdaptive
ReadyBefore any contactAfter a first contact with a specific antigen
PartsBarriers, low pH, lysozyme, thiocyanate, interferons, phagocytes, NK cellsB cells (humoral, antibodies) and T cells (cellular)
ResultNonspecific defenseAcquired resistance, often with memory

Watch for: Antibodies are adaptive (the humoral arm), never innate. The cellular arm doesn't work through antibodies. Thiocyanate in saliva is innate, not made by B or T cells. NK cells are lymphocytes but innate: his slide calls them "(Killer T cells)", yet they lack the B and T markers; the killer T cells are the CD8 cytotoxic T cells of adaptive immunity.

items.h: General roles of B cells, T cells, and NK cells
items.body:
B cells make antibody (humoral), T cells read antigen held up on MHC and either help or kill (cellular), and NK cells kill altered cells with no antigen receptor at all (innate). He kept it to the general roles.

Know this
  • B cells display membrane-bound IgM and IgD as their antigen receptors, one antigen per cell. When its antibody fits an antigen, the B cell recruits helper T cells and becomes a plasma cell that releases that antibody into the circulation: plasma cell means "antibody production and release."
  • B cells become plasma cells in the secondary lymphoid organs, driven by lymphokines from helper T cells.
  • T cells carry no antibodies; the T cell receptor (TCR) sees antigen only when it is bound to MHC. T cells take part in immunologic memory.
  • Helper T (CD4): antigen on MHC class II, shown by antigen-presenting cells such as macrophages; its interleukins and lymphokines drive B, T and NK cells. They are "what's going to help our B lymphocytes."
  • Cytotoxic T (CD8): antigen on MHC class I (virus-infected and altered cells); perforins lyse the cell; allograft rejection and tumor immunology. They are "probably just gonna kill whatever they bind." Cue: CD4 times MHC 2 and CD8 times MHC 1 both make 8.
  • NK cells: the large lymphocytes, with no B or T markers and no antigen-specific receptor; innate; they kill tumor and virus-infected cells. Markers include CD16, CD56, CD94.
  • The NK decision: an activating receptor binds an activating ligand, and an inhibitory receptor binds MHC class I. A healthy cell shows both: no killing. A cell missing MHC class I: killed. Far more activating ligands than usual: induced killing even with MHC class I (probably part of autoimmunity).
  • ADCC: circulating antibodies bind antigens on the target; Fc receptors on NK cells, macrophages, neutrophils and eosinophils bind them (the NK cell's CD16 binds the constant region of IgG); the killers release perforins, granzymes, TNF and lytic enzymes. No TCR and no MHC.

Watch for: Helper T cells help; perforins are the CD8 cell's. B cells use IgM and IgD, not a TCR; only T cells need antigen on MHC. A healthy cell carries the activating ligand too: its MHC class I is what spares it. He once said "MHC class 2" for the NK target; NK cells check MHC class I, as the keys say. He also said "IgG" aloud for antibodies in general; the keys put IgM and IgD on the B cell. Said not needed: how helper and cytotoxic T cells respond differently.

items.h: Primary vs. secondary lymphoid organs
items.body:
Primary organs make lymphocytes immunocompetent before they ever meet antigen; secondary organs are where they meet it and go to work. For this class: "bone marrow, B cells, thymus, T cells," and any other lymphoid organ is secondary.

Know this
  • Primary: the bone marrow and the thymus only. They make B and T cells immunocompetent in the absence of antigen. GALT is not primary (his figure lists it there; he struck it).
  • Bone marrow: B cells and NK cells form and mature there; stromal cells make the cytokines that govern B cell development; self-reactive B cells are eliminated; B cells leave with one antigen-specific IgM or IgD.
  • T cell precursors leave the marrow immunoincompetent (CD4 and CD8 negative), mature in the thymus, and leave it CD4 or CD8 positive.
  • Secondary: the lymph nodes (filter lymph), MALT and GALT (tonsils, Peyer's patches, appendix; the first defense against external antigens) and the spleen (filters blood). They capture antigen and activate B and T cells, which undergo clonal proliferation into effector cells.
  • Stroma: reticular cells and reticulin (type III collagen) in every lymphoid organ except the thymus, whose stroma is epithelioreticular cells ("I do want you to know that").
  • MALT: lymphocytes and unencapsulated nodules in the lamina propria of the GI, respiratory and genitourinary tracts; B cells in the nodules, T cells around them (the interfollicular regions of the Peyer's patches); its antibody is IgA, actively transported into the lumen.
  • Peyer's patches are in the ileum, under M cells that ferry antigens from the lumen to the B cells and CD4 T cells below.
  • Waldeyer's ring of tonsils: pharyngeal (back of the nasal cavity), tubal (at the torus tubarius, where the auditory tube opens), palatine (back of the throat; their crypts trap material, so the tissue has longer to respond) and lingual (back of the tongue). No afferent lymphatics; they fight bacteria and viruses with immunoglobulins from plasma cells.
  • Adenoiditis: a child's enlarged, inflamed pharyngeal tonsil, which can obstruct breathing (mouth breathing).

Watch for: GALT, the tonsils and the Peyer's patches are all secondary. Self-reactive B cells are removed in the marrow, not the thymus. Reticulin is type III collagen (he said "type 2" once; type I is the wrong answer in the bank). The pharyngeal tonsil is in the nasopharynx; the lingual tonsils are on the tongue. Said not needed: the long list of tissues on his overview figure and the colony-forming unit sentence.

items.h: Basic organization and function of the thymus, lymph node, and spleen
items.body:
The thymus trains T cells, the lymph node filters lymph, and the spleen filters blood, each with its own B and T cell zones. When a question describes a region instead of naming it, find its landmark (the table).

Know this
  • Thymus: bilobed, behind the manubrium (superior and anterior mediastinum). Largest and most active in the newborn; by the teens it involutes and fat replaces it, which is normal (the fat in front of an adult's heart).
  • Its epithelioreticular cells come from endoderm (pharyngeal pouches), its capsule and trabeculae from mesoderm, which carry efferent, not afferent, lymphatics. Each lobule has a cortex and a medulla.
  • Cortex: densely packed developing T cells, so it stains darker; macrophages clear the failures. Medulla: looser, bigger T cells, more epithelioreticular cells, lighter, with Hassall's corpuscles.
  • T cell receptor genes are rearranged here, and 95 to 99 percent of thymocytes are selected out and die by apoptosis.
  • Thymic education, in order: in through postcapillary venules; out to the cortex, gaining the TCR, CD3, CD4 and CD8; positive selection in the cortex; negative selection in the medulla (removes cells aimed at self antigen on self MHC); out through postcapillary venules as CD4 or CD8 cells (one or the other, not both).
  • Blood-thymus barrier: the capillary endothelium and its basement membrane, perivascular connective tissue with macrophages, and epithelioreticular cells. It shields developing T cells from blood antigens.
  • Lymph node: encapsulated; it filters lymph, produces lymphocytes, makes antibody (mostly IgG) and recirculates lymphocytes.
  • Cortex: B cell follicles. Paracortex (deep cortex): T cells. A primary follicle is B cells with no germinal center; after antigen, a secondary follicle has a germinal center (B cells proliferate) in a mantle zone.
  • Lymph runs afferent lymphatic, subcapsular sinus, trabecular sinuses, efferent lymphatic: the only lymphoid structure with both. Lymphocytes from the blood enter through high endothelial venules in the deep cortex.
  • An antigen's trip: in by the afferent lymphatic; initial T and B activation in the paracortex; B activation in a primary follicle; B proliferation in the germinal center; plasma cells secrete antibody in the medulla; out the efferent lymphatic. A tender node under the jaw after a tooth infection: antigen in the afferent lymph, B cells multiplying in the germinal centers of the cortex.
  • Dendritic cells present antigen to T cells. Follicular dendritic cells hold antigen-antibody complexes (Fc receptors) among germinal center B cells but lack MHC II, so they are not antigen-presenting cells.
  • Lymphatic capillaries are blind-ended, permeable and lack a basal lamina; lymph drains by the thoracic duct into the subclavian veins.
  • Spleen: the largest lymphoid organ, upper left quadrant behind the stomach; it filters blood. The splenic artery (from the celiac trunk) brings blood-borne antigens in at the hilum; no afferent lymphatics (efferent ones leave at the hilum).
  • Its jobs: clears aged and defective red cells and platelets and microbes, recycles iron, stores about a third of the platelets, makes plasma cells and IgM and IgG.
  • White pulp, around a central arteriole: the PALS of T cells, B cell nodules farther out, and the marginal zone around it all (macrophages and some B cells). Red pulp, most of the spleen: splenic cords and venous sinusoids.
  • In the open circulation, sheathed capillaries empty into the cords' meshwork; macrophages sample the blood, and the cells squeeze through slits back into the sinuses (closed: straight into the sinuses).
  • Splenic sinuses: rod-shaped, loosely packed endothelial cells with slits, macrophage processes between them, hoops of basal lamina strands, and no smooth muscle, no pericytes.
ThymusLymph nodeSpleen
TypePrimarySecondarySecondary
Main jobTrains T cellsFilters lymphFilters blood

B cellsNot its jobCortex folliclesWhite pulp nodules; marginal zone
T cellsCortex, then medullaParacortexPALS
LandmarkHassall's corpuscles (medulla)High endothelial venules (paracortex)Central arteriole with its PALS

Watch for: PALS means the spleen and T cells. A primary follicle has no germinal center. Clearing old red cells is the spleen's job, not the node's, and the spleen doesn't educate T cells. Red pulp, not white, is most of the spleen. Follicular dendritic cells are no part of the blood-thymus barrier. He called the spleen's regions "the cortex, and ... kind of a medulla area"; the texts say it has neither, and the bank keys white pulp and red pulp. His circulation slide put "(PALS)" after the sheathed capillaries; the PALS is around the central arteriole, where he put it aloud. Know what the open and closed routes are; no question asks which is more common.

terms.d: The most common white cell (50 to 70 percent), with a multi-lobed nucleus: the main phagocyte of the blood and the first line of defense against bacteria, in the blood about 10 hours.

A white cell (1 to 4 percent) with a bilobed nucleus and granules red with eosin; its major basic protein disrupts parasite membranes, and it rises in parasitic infections and allergies such as hay fever.

The natural killer cell: a large lymphocyte of innate immunity with no B or T markers and no antigen-specific receptor. It kills cells missing MHC class I (tumor and virus-infected cells), and its CD16 binds IgG's constant region for ADCC.

The primary lymphoid organ where T cells mature, behind the manubrium, with an epithelioreticular stroma, a dark cortex (positive selection) and a lighter medulla (negative selection, Hassall's corpuscles); it involutes to fat by the teens.
The other primary lymphoid organ and the source of every blood cell in an adult: B and NK cells mature there and self-reactive B cells are eliminated, while T cell precursors leave it for the thymus.

The largest lymphoid organ, a secondary one that filters blood, with no afferent lymphatics: white pulp (PALS and B cell nodules) and red pulp (cords and sinusoids). It clears old red cells and platelets and stores a third of the platelets.
The periarteriolar lymphatic sheath: T cells around the central arteriole of the spleen's white pulp. "Associate this PALS with the spleen."

items.h: How the major leukemias are classified
items.body:
Leukemia is a cancer of the blood-forming cells: neoplastic cells replace the normal bone marrow and blood. Dr. Borak sorts every leukemia on two axes, acute or chronic (do the cells still mature?) and myeloid or lymphoid (which line?), which gives the four major leukemias.

Know this
  • Leukemia frequently starts in the bone marrow and can spread to the spleen, liver and lymph nodes; untreated it is fatal. His short version: lymphoma generally involves the nodes, leukemia the marrow and the blood.
  • Acute = blasts that don't mature; chronic = cells that still mature. Myeloid = granulocytes (neutrophils) and monocytes; lymphoid = B and T cells.
  • AML = acute myeloid (adults); ALL = acute lymphoblastic, B-ALL or T-ALL (young children); CML = chronic myeloid; CLL = chronic lymphocytic, small mature B cells.
  • Blasts are the hallmark of acute leukemia: more than 20 percent in the blood or the marrow makes the diagnosis ("that's our threshold"). An AML with a defining genetic abnormality is diagnosed at any blast count.
  • Blasts in the peripheral blood are always abnormal, except in newborns.
  • The workup: a blood count flags blasts, a peripheral smear checks for them, then the bone marrow is sampled (aspirate and core biopsy). Posterior iliac crest: both, in adults; sternum: aspirate only (the heart is below); tibia: aspirate only, in small children.
  • Acute leukemia can arise de novo or grow out of another marrow disorder: myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), CML, a myeloproliferative neoplasm, earlier chemotherapy or radiation, or Down syndrome.
  • MDS: persistent cytopenias with abnormal-looking precursors and blasts under 20 percent; it can progress to AML.
MyeloidLymphoid
AcuteAMLALL
ChronicCMLCLL

Watch for: CLL is lymphoid, not myeloid; "acute and lymphoid" is ALL; and ALL, not AML, is the acute leukemia of young children. An older patient with a year of low counts, abnormal-looking precursors and 8 percent blasts has MDS, not AML. "Greater than 20 percent" is his wording (the WHO's is 20 percent or more): the number is 20. The AML subtypes (M0 to M7) were said not to be needed.

items.h: Acute vs. chronic disease
items.body:
Acute leukemia is blasts that don't mature, so the marrow fills and fails fast. Chronic leukemia is cells that still mature, so the count climbs slowly, the spleen fills and the platelets hold up until late. His comparison uses CML, "the main chronic leukemia that you need to know"; CLL is the chronic lymphoid one.

Know this
  • Acute: rapid onset, under 6 months untreated, blasts over 20 percent, platelets low to very low, mild organomegaly.
  • CML: insidious onset, 2 to 6 years untreated, mature cells with blasts under 20 percent, a high white count, mild anemia, platelets normal or high early, then low, prominent organomegaly.
  • Untreated, both end in death by infection or bleeding.
  • CML: t(9;22), the Philadelphia chromosome, makes BCR-ABL1, a tyrosine kinase always on. The blood: a very high count (median about 80,000/µL) of neutrophils at every stage of maturation, peaking at myelocytes and segmented neutrophils, not mainly blasts.
  • More than 95 percent of CML is found in the chronic phase, often on a routine count, with the cells in the blood, marrow, spleen and liver. Untreated, a blast phase follows in a few years, when blasts infiltrate the skin, soft tissues, nodes and other sites.
  • Imatinib (Gleevec) competes with ATP at the active site of the BCR-ABL1 (p210) kinase, so it can't activate.
  • CLL/SLL is one disease of small, mature B cells: blood = CLL, node = SLL. CLL needs at least 5 × 109/L of these B cells; below that, with no tissue disease, it is monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis, a pre-neoplastic process.
  • CLL: 70 or older; soccer-ball chromatin and smudge cells; infections from hypogammaglobulinemia; slow but largely incurable.
AcuteCML
Onset, courseRapid, under 6 monthsInsidious, 2 to 6 years
CellsBlasts over 20%Mature, blasts under 20%
PlateletsLow to very lowNormal or high, then low
OrgansMild organomegalyProminent organomegaly
DeathInfection or bleedingInfection or bleeding

Watch for: "Mostly mature cells with fewer than 20 percent blasts" describes chronic, not acute, leukemia, and CML's onset is insidious, not rapid. Skin and soft-tissue infiltration is CML's blast phase, not its chronic phase. "SLL is a different disease" and "targeted therapy cures most CLL" are false. His slide put acute leukemia in children, but he corrected it aloud: that is ALL; AML is mostly adults.

items.h: Myeloid vs. lymphoid disease
items.body:
Every blood cell comes from the marrow's stem cell down a myeloid or a lymphoid line, and a tumor looks like the normal cell it comes from. Myeloid cells mostly become leukemias; lymphoid cells become lymphomas or leukemias. In acute leukemia, AML vs. ALL is the split, and an Auer rod settles it.

Know this
  • Myeloid line: red cells, platelets, granulocytes and monocytes. Lymphoid line: B, T and NK cells; B cells become plasma cells.
  • Myeloid disease: AML (with APL and acute monocytic leukemia), CML, MDS. Lymphoid disease: ALL, CLL/SLL, the lymphomas, the plasma cell neoplasms.
  • The neutrophil line, in order: myeloblast, promyelocyte (granules appear), myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band, segmented neutrophil (PMN). In leukemia, maturation stalls.
  • AML: mostly adults (median 65); medium to large blasts with granules, distinct nucleoli and maybe Auer rods.
  • ALL: mostly children, usually 1 to 5, with a poor prognosis under 1; small blasts with scant cytoplasm, no granules, indistinct nucleoli.
  • Auer rod: a red-blue, needle-like inclusion of fused granules in a myeloblast. It means myeloid: Auer rods exclude ALL.
  • B-ALL is the most common leukemia of childhood; over 90 percent of children reach long-term remission. T-ALL often brings a mediastinal mass and looks the same as B-ALL: testing shows the T cells. Only ALL's demographics were said to be needed.
  • APL: t(15;17) fuses PML with RARA; maturation stops at the promyelocyte; large granules and bundles of Auer rods.
  • Acute monocytic leukemia: blasts with kidney-shaped (reniform) nuclei; it can show in the gums.
  • Flow cytometry shows the line (B, T or myeloid; mature or blast); the CD markers were said not to be needed.
AMLALL
WhoAdults, median 65Children, 1 to 5
BlastsMedium to largeSmall to medium
CytoplasmGranulesScant, no granules
NucleoliDistinctIndistinct
Auer rodsCan be presentNever

Watch for: "Lymphoblasts carry granules and Auer rods" is false, and small cells with scant cytoplasm and indistinct nucleoli are lymphoblasts, not myeloblasts. Right after the promyelocyte comes the myelocyte (aloud he skipped the metamyelocyte; his slide has it before the band). Retinoic acid lets APL's promyelocytes mature; imatinib blocks CML's kinase.

items.h: Major differences between Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma
items.body:
Hodgkin lymphoma is a few huge, bizarre tumor cells in a crowd of normal immune cells, usually localized and spreading node to node. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, mostly B-cell, looks like normal lymphocytes, is usually widespread and often starts outside the nodes.

Know this
  • Hodgkin: usually localized; starts in central nodes (the chest); spreads contiguously, node to node; extranodal disease uncommon; the blood never involved.
  • Non-Hodgkin: usually widespread; peripheral nodes or outside the nodes; can skip node groups (above and below the diaphragm, the node between not enlarged); can involve the blood.
  • Reed-Sternberg cells: a small fraction of the mass, very large, two nuclear lobes with prominent pink nucleoli (owl's eye), in a reactive background; with the one-nucleus Hodgkin cells, the HRS cells. "That's the main thing that you need to recognize."
  • Classic Hodgkin: painless, firm nodes above the diaphragm (cervical, supraclavicular, mediastinal); rare but distinctive node pain after alcohol; EBV drives some cases; over 80 percent cured.
  • B symptoms, "really high-yield clues": fever 38 °C or higher; drenching night sweats; at least 10 percent weight loss in 6 months. They raise suspicion: the tissue makes the diagnosis.
  • Staging: one site or several; one or both sides of the diaphragm; extranodal sites; disseminated (marrow, liver) = stage 4, "the most aggressive". B after the stage means B symptoms.
HodgkinNon-Hodgkin
When foundLocalizedWidespread
StartsCentral nodesPeripheral nodes, extranodal
SpreadContiguousCan skip
ExtranodalUncommonMuch more common
BloodNeverCan be involved
Tumor cellsFew, bizarre (Reed-Sternberg)Like normal lymphocytes
TreatmentABVDOften CHOP

Watch for: "Hodgkin often involves the blood" and "often starts outside the nodes" are false. Bone pain isn't a B symptom, and the weight loss is 10 percent in 6 months, not 5 percent in a year. B symptoms don't make stage 4; nodes on both sides of the diaphragm are stage III (the standard chart; he named only stage 4). Look-alikes: a starry sky is Burkitt; sheets of large B cells are DLBCL. Aloud he put Hodgkin's start in the chest; his slide says the neck: both are above the diaphragm, and no key depends on it. The Hodgkin subtypes were said not to be needed.

items.h: Recognizing important lymphoma categories and associations
items.body:
His closing request: "I want you to know generally kind of what category things are" (B-cell or T-cell, indolent or aggressive) and "the molecular associations on the ones that are sort of underlined", cyclin D1 included. Each lymphoma resembles the normal cell it comes from.

Know this
  • The tissue makes the diagnosis. A lymphoma node's architecture is effaced by one monotonous population (a benign node: rubbery, separate follicles, open sinuses). Only kappa or only lambda (normal about 3 to 1) means a clonal population.
  • 85 to 90 percent of lymphoid neoplasms are B-cell; NK-cell ones are rare.
  • Counterparts: germinal center = follicular; mantle zone = mantle cell; marginal zone = marginal zone lymphoma.
  • Indolent B-cell: CLL/SLL, follicular, mantle cell, marginal zone. Aggressive B-cell: DLBCL, Burkitt. T or NK-cell: mycosis fungoides (indolent); peripheral T-cell, Sézary syndrome, extranodal NK/T-cell (aggressive).
  • Follicular: back-to-back follicles; t(14;18) keeps BCL2 on, so the cells don't die; widespread at diagnosis yet often without symptoms (B symptoms uncommon); median survival over 17 years; the prognosis follows how far it had spread.
  • Mantle cell: t(11;14) switches on cyclin D1, and "nothing else in the lymphomas will do that": a cyclin D1 stain = mantle cell (it separates it from CLL/SLL); older adults, enlarged nodes; median survival up from 3 years to more than 5 to 10.
  • Marginal zone (MALT), "the one you guys are going to experience the most": indolent, extranodal, grown from chronic inflammation: stomach, H. pylori; ocular adnexa, Chlamydia psittaci; skin, Borrelia; salivary gland, Sjögren; thyroid, Hashimoto. Key finding: lymphoepithelial lesions; B symptoms rare.
  • DLBCL: about 30 percent of adult lymphomas; large cells in sheets; a rapidly enlarging node or mass; arises de novo or from an indolent lymphoma.
  • Burkitt: very aggressive; t(8;14) puts MYC next to IGH; starry sky = tingible-body macrophages eating apoptotic debris (the key finding); endemic: African children, the jaw, EBV; about 90 percent of children survive.
  • EBV: Burkitt, extranodal NK/T-cell, EBV-positive classic Hodgkin. Not follicular, mantle cell or gastric MALT.
  • Mycosis fungoides: the most common skin lymphoma, indolent T-cell; patches, then plaques, then tumors. Sézary syndrome, its aggressive form: erythroderma, generalized lymphadenopathy, cerebriform Sézary cells in the blood.
  • Peripheral T-cell: very aggressive, B symptoms, poor response to chemotherapy. Extranodal NK/T-cell: the nose, EBV, destroyed vessels and necrosis, a perforated hard palate; mainly eastern Asia.
  • Plasma cell neoplasms: plasmacytoma = solitary; multiple myeloma = multifocal in the marrow, an M-spike, CRAB (hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, lytic bone) and rouleaux from the excess immunoglobulin.
TranslocationGenesDisease
t(14;18)BCL2, IGHFollicular
t(11;14)Cyclin D1, IGHMantle cell
t(8;14)MYC, IGHBurkitt
t(9;22)BCR-ABL1CML
t(15;17)PML-RARAAPL

Watch for: each translocation's distractors are the other four; mantle cell is the mantle zone, not the marginal zone; the ocular adnexa go with Chlamydia, the skin with Borrelia, the thyroid with Hashimoto, not Sjögren. A mediastinal mass is not Sézary (it is T-lymphoblastic lymphoma). Myeloma's calcium is high; its jaw lesions can mimic the brown tumors of hyperparathyroidism, but the M-spike and rouleaux point to myeloma. He grouped mantle cell as indolent (textbooks: aggressive), and once swapped Burkitt's endemic and sporadic forms aloud (the hub follows his slide); no key depends on either.

items.h: Common clinical consequences of leukemia
items.body:
Leukemia does harm two ways: its cells crowd normal blood-making out of the marrow (marrow failure), and they grow in tissues (organ infiltration). Both show in the mouth: "you guys may actually be the clue that a patient has leukemia that's not detected."

Know this
  • Marrow failure, "particularly anemia": anemia (fatigue, malaise, pallor); low platelets (bruising, bleeding, petechiae); too few working white cells (fever, infections).
  • Organ infiltration: bone and joint pain ("should point you toward leukemia"); splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy; CNS symptoms; gingival hypertrophy.
  • Acute monocytic leukemia can present outside the marrow in the gums: leukemic cells infiltrate them (a myeloid sarcoma). Swollen gums with fatigue, pallor and bruising: get a blood count.
  • APL: a coagulopathy and DIC ("you clot everywhere at the same time") that can cause early death; bleeding gums and petechiae. All-trans retinoic acid with arsenic trioxide, without conventional chemotherapy, is largely curative (low- and intermediate-risk APL).
  • CLL: infections from hypogammaglobulinemia (too little normal antibody), not from blasts.
  • Untreated, leukemia is fatal, by infection or bleeding. Treatment aims to eradicate the leukemic cells and give supportive care; the goal is complete remission (no disease, normal counts).
Marrow failureOrgan infiltration
Pallor, fatigueBone pain
Bruising, bleeding gumsBig spleen, liver, nodes
Fever, infectionsSwollen gums

Watch for: gingival hypertrophy is the EXCEPT among marrow-failure signs: it is infiltration. Swollen gums in a leukemic patient are leukemic cells, not plaque gingivitis or bleeding from low platelets. APL's emergency is DIC, not a mediastinal mass (T-lymphoblastic lymphoma), high calcium (myeloma) or skin infiltration (CML's blast phase).

terms.d: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia: an acute leukemia of lymphoid blasts (B-ALL, the most common leukemia of childhood, or T-ALL), mostly in children 1 to 5, with a poor prognosis under 1. Small blasts, no granules, never Auer rods.

Acute myeloid leukemia: an acute leukemia of myeloid blasts, mostly in adults (median 65), diagnosed by more than 20 percent blasts, or any count with a defining genetic abnormality; Auer rods. The two to know: APL (t(15;17), DIC) and acute monocytic (the gums).

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia: small, mature B cells, the same disease as SLL, with at least 5 × 109/L in the blood. Patients 70 or older; soccer-ball chromatin and smudge cells; infections from hypogammaglobulinemia; slow but largely incurable.

Chronic myeloid leukemia, the chronic leukemia he said to know: t(9;22), the Philadelphia chromosome, makes BCR-ABL1, a kinase always on. A very high count of neutrophils at every stage, few blasts, a big spleen; imatinib.

The large tumor cells of classic Hodgkin lymphoma: two nuclear lobes with prominent pink nucleoli (owl's eyes), a few scattered among reactive immune cells. Recognizing them is "the main thing" in Hodgkin.

A very aggressive B-cell lymphoma: t(8;14) (MYC with IGH) and a starry sky of macrophages eating debris. Endemic in African children's jaws, with EBV; about 90 percent of children survive with chemotherapy.
A B-cell lymphoma of the mantle zone with t(11;14) and cyclin D1: a cyclin D1 stain means mantle cell. Older adults with enlarged nodes; survival much improved.

Mycosis fungoides: the most common skin lymphoma, an indolent T-cell lymphoma (patches, plaques, tumors). Sézary syndrome: its aggressive form, with erythroderma, generalized lymphadenopathy and cerebriform Sézary cells in the blood.

items.h: Disorders of testicular development/descent
items.body:
The testes develop in the retroperitoneum and descend through the inguinal canal into the scrotum before birth, because making sperm needs a place cooler than the body. The guide's disorder is cryptorchidism, a testis that never came down; the same path explains the lecture's two emergencies.

Know this
  • Cryptorchidism ("crypto means hidden"): a testis that isn't in the scrotum, left in the retroperitoneum or the inguinal canal.
  • The testes develop retroperitoneally and descend through the inguinal canal. The scrotum keeps them about 2 degrees below body temperature: spermatogenesis "likes cool weather."
  • An undescended testis sits at body temperature (37 °C), and the heat halts spermatogenesis: the cause of infertility and testicular cancer.
  • Wait through the first year, up to the second; if it hasn't come down by about 2 years, surgery brings it into the scrotum.
  • Surgery prevents the infertility, but the testicular cancer risk stays: "cryptorchidism is a predisposing factor to testicular cancer," the closing reminder. The lecture tied it to seminoma by name.
  • Testicular atrophy (as in infertility): tubules with only Sertoli cells, no spermatogonia or spermatids, and a thickened basement membrane.
  • Inguinal hernia: the canal can stay open in the first years of life; a loop of bowel trapped in it can infarct, so it is an emergency.
  • Testicular torsion: a loose spermatic cord twists and cuts off the blood supply, and the testis can infarct. A medical emergency, though losing one testis won't by itself cause infertility.
  • Developmental anomalies of the penis: in hypospadias the urethra opens on the ventral side (underneath), in epispadias on the dorsal side (on top).
What it isEmergency?
CryptorchidismA testis that never descendedNo: surgery by about 2 years
TorsionA twisted cord; the testis infarctsYes
Inguinal herniaBowel trapped in the open canalYes
HydroceleFluid between the two layers of the tunica vaginalisNo: a common swelling

Watch for: Heat halts spermatogenesis; it doesn't speed it up. After surgery, the risk that stays is cancer, not infertility. The lecture's numbers (about 1 in 10 newborns, surgery at about 2 years) differ from the textbooks (about 3 percent, corrected by about 18 months); no question depends on either.

items.h: Major categories of testicular tumors
items.body:
Almost all testicular tumors come from the germ cells. Dr. Dal Zotto said the classification "is going to be simple" for you: germ cell tumors against the rest, and within them, seminoma against the non-seminomatous tumors, because seminoma responds to radiotherapy and the others don't respond as well.

Know this
  • Inside the seminiferous tubules: the germ cells (spermatogonia) and the Sertoli cells, which conduct their maturation. Outside: the Leydig cells, which secrete testosterone. Sertoli and Leydig cells are sex cord-stromal cells, not germ cells.
  • 95 percent of testicular tumors are germ cell tumors, from the spermatogonia, and they are cured in more than 95 percent of cases.
  • The rest: sex cord-stromal tumors (Sertoli and Leydig cell tumors) or mixed tumors; in older men, lymphoma involving the testis secondarily, and metastases.
  • The risk factor to know: cryptorchidism. The incidence varies by country (Norway highest) and, unlike penile cancer, is not tied to low socioeconomic status.
  • Seminoma, the most frequent: young adults (30s and 40s); white, multinodular and solid, with no hemorrhage and no necrosis; associated with cryptorchidism.
  • Seminoma usually has no serum tumor marker, so a pathologist makes the diagnosis. It behaves very well and responds to radiotherapy.
  • Non-seminomatous: embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma and teratoma, which recapitulate fetal tissues. More aggressive (choriocarcinoma most of all), and they don't respond as well to radiotherapy.
SeminomaNon-seminomatous
MembersSeminomaEmbryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, teratoma
FrequencyThe most frequentLess frequent
BehaviorVery goodMore aggressive
RadiotherapyRespondsDoesn't respond as well

Watch for: Leydig and Sertoli cell tumors are sex cord-stromal, never germ cell tumors. A non-germ cell tumor in an older man is often a secondary lymphoma. Said not needed ("general information"): the full classification, the seminoma's look under the microscope and each non-seminomatous tumor's features, such as choriocarcinoma's beta-hCG, which wrong choices mention. A young adult with a white, solid tumor, no hemorrhage or necrosis and no marker has a seminoma.

items.h: Common infections of the male reproductive tract
items.body:
The lecture's infections run from the outside in: the glans and foreskin, the epididymis and, rarely, the testis itself. HPV is the one the lecture stressed: its low-risk types make a benign wart, its high-risk types a premalignant lesion, and a tight foreskin (phimosis) sets the stage for infection and penile carcinoma.

Know this
  • The glans and prepuce (foreskin): a nonspecific infection, such as bacterial, or a sexually transmitted one: syphilis, gonorrhea or chlamydia.
  • Epididymitis: sexually transmitted gonorrhea or chlamydia, or a urinary tract infection that spreads to it.
  • Orchitis, of the testis itself, is very uncommon: viral, syphilis (Treponema pallidum), tuberculosis, brucellosis.
  • Condyloma acuminatum: HPV 6 and 11, the low-risk types. Benign, sexually transmitted, very contagious (the virus stays latent even without lesions); white and verrucous, on the glans and foreskin or anywhere on the anogenital skin.
  • Penile intraepithelial neoplasia (PeIN), premalignant: HPV-associated, the more frequent, from the high-risk types 16 and 18; or HPV-independent, in men over 60 with chronic inflammation and lichen sclerosus.
  • "The lower numbers, 6 and 11, are benign. Higher numbers, 16 and 18, are premalignant." 30 percent of PeIN become invasive if untreated. PeIN is flat and reddish, not verrucous like a condyloma.
  • Phimosis, a foreskin that can't be retracted (very common in toddlers): the fold fills with smegma, then infection, chronic inflammation and carcinoma of the penis (the closing reminder).
  • Penile squamous cell carcinoma: rare in the United States, tied to poor hygiene, phimosis and lower socioeconomic status; indolent, spreading to the inguinal lymph nodes but not much further.
WhereCauses
Glans and foreskinNonspecific bacteria; syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia
EpididymisGonorrhea, chlamydia; a spreading UTI
Testis (orchitis, very uncommon)Viruses, syphilis, tuberculosis, brucellosis
Anogenital skinHPV 6 and 11: condyloma. HPV 16 and 18: PeIN

Watch for: Orchitis is the rare one: a choice calling it more common than epididymitis is false. Condyloma doesn't predispose to carcinoma; 16 and 18 (or lichen sclerosus) do. Phimosis predisposes to penile carcinoma, cryptorchidism to testicular cancer: don't swap them.

items.h: Major benign and malignant prostate disorders
items.body:
The prostate has two big diseases, and where each starts predicts how it behaves. BPH, benign, grows around the urethra, so it blocks the urine; prostatic adenocarcinoma, malignant, starts in the peripheral zone, so it doesn't obstruct early. The cancer is found by PSA, spreads to bone and is graded by Gleason.

Know this
  • The prostate: about 20 grams, below the bladder, the urethra running through it. It makes glycoproteins such as PSA (prostate-specific antigen) that keep the sperm nourished and moving.
  • The zones predict the disease: BPH arises around the urethra (the transition, or periurethral, zone); carcinoma in the peripheral zone, toward the back.
  • BPH: hyperplasia of both the glands and the stroma, in nearly every man after 50 ("you cannot avoid this"); it obstructs the urethra, so urinating is hard. Hormones play a role; surgery treats severe obstruction. It wasn't taught as a precursor of carcinoma.
  • Prostatic adenocarcinoma: the most frequent cancer in men, in men over 65; from the peripheral zone, it doesn't obstruct early.
  • It is found by serum PSA, a simple blood draw: its glands make much more PSA than normal ones (the lecture said 10 times).
  • It "likes the bones": its bone metastases form bone (osteoblastic). An osteoblastic lesion in a man means: think prostate, order a PSA.
  • Gleason grading grades differentiation, from well-differentiated glands to masses of tumor and single cells; the worse the differentiation, the worse the prognosis.
BPHAdenocarcinoma
WhereAround the urethraPeripheral zone
What growsGlands and stroma, benignMalignant glands
UrineObstructedNot obstructed early
WhoNearly every man after 50Men over 65
Found bySymptomsSerum PSA
SpreadNoneBone, osteoblastic

Watch for: Don't swap the zones. Gleason grades differentiation, not depth (depth stages a bladder carcinoma) or PSA. Painless hematuria points to bladder (urothelial) carcinoma, not the prostate. The lecture called the area around the urethra both the "central zone" and the "transitional zone"; the central zone is a separate zone in anatomy, so the questions say "around the urethra" or "transition zone".

terms.d: A testis that never descended into the scrotum ("crypto means hidden"). Body heat halts spermatogenesis, so infertility and testicular cancer; surgery at about 2 years prevents the infertility, but the cancer risk stays.

Tumors of the spermatogonia: 95 percent of testicular tumors, cured in more than 95 percent, predisposed by cryptorchidism. They split into seminoma and the non-seminomatous tumors (embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, teratoma).

The most frequent testicular germ cell tumor, in young adults (30s and 40s): white, multinodular and solid with no hemorrhage or necrosis, usually no serum marker. It behaves very well and responds to radiotherapy.
Benign prostatic hyperplasia: hyperplasia of the glands and stroma around the urethra (transition zone), in nearly every man after 50. It obstructs the urine; surgery treats the severe cases.
The most frequent cancer in men (over 65), from the peripheral zone, so no early obstruction. Found by serum PSA; its bone metastases are osteoblastic; graded by Gleason.
The grade of a prostatic adenocarcinoma's differentiation, from well-differentiated glands to poorly differentiated masses and single cells; the worse the differentiation, the worse the prognosis.

items.h: Common disorders of the vulva, vagina, and cervix
items.body:
The cervix's disorders start at its transformation zone (the HPV item); the vagina's most common one is inflammation, vaginitis; the vulva has three non-infectious "lichens", HPV warts and squamous cell carcinoma. Dr. Dal Zotto paused on lichen sclerosus "because this is important": it is the one that leads to cancer.

Know this
  • Cervix: glandular endocervix, non-keratinizing squamous ectocervix, and between them the transformation zone, inflamed, open to HPV and where cervical cancer arises.
  • Vagina: vaginitis is its most frequent non-neoplastic condition ("everybody has in their life vaginitis"): Candida, Trichomonas, or atrophic in older women. Its tumors: VaIN and squamous cell carcinoma (reproductive age), and sarcoma botryoides (girls under 5).
  • Lichen simplex chronicus: vulvar skin thickened and leathery (hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, acanthosis) from continuous scratching and rubbing, a reaction to anything that itches.
  • Lichen sclerosus: unknown cause (postulated autoimmune). A completely atrophic epithelium over dermal sclerosis and hyalinization; the vulva looks smooth, like parchment paper. It itches, so lichen simplex chronicus can form on top.
  • Lichen sclerosus is "the single non-infectious inflammatory disorder that can lead to carcinomas": the HPV-independent vulvar squamous cell carcinoma of women over 60. Diagnose and treat it in time.
  • Lichen planus ("because you're going to be dentists"): vulvar and oral lesions together; painful erosions with many lymphocytes in the dermis. A biopsy sent fresh, not in formalin, for immunofluorescence makes the diagnosis; steroids treat it.
  • Condyloma acuminatum: HPV 6 and 11, benign; finger-like, wart-like, with koilocytes.
  • Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma: HPV-associated (16 and 18; better prognosis, radiosensitive) or HPV-independent (older women, lichen sclerosus).

Watch for: Thick and leathery is lichen simplex chronicus; thin and parchment-like is lichen sclerosus; erosions with mouth lesions are lichen planus. Lichen sclerosus's carcinoma is the HPV-independent one, not the HPV 16 and 18 kind. The ectocervix is non-keratinizing.

items.h: Distinguishing neoplastic from non-neoplastic lesions
items.body:
Sort each lesion by what it is: inflammation and infection are non-neoplastic; a proliferation of abnormal cells (an intraepithelial neoplasia, a carcinoma, a sarcoma) is neoplastic. Neither word settles the risk alone: an inflammatory lichen can lead to cancer, and a neoplastic lesion stays in situ until it invades the stroma.

Know this
  • Non-neoplastic: vaginitis (Candida, Trichomonas, atrophic), the vulva's lichen simplex chronicus, lichen sclerosus and lichen planus, and the inflamed transformation zone.
  • Neoplastic: the cervix's squamous intraepithelial lesions (low and high grade; CIN), vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia (VaIN), squamous cell carcinoma, and sarcoma botryoides.
  • In situ lesions are confined to the epithelium; once one invades the stroma, it is squamous cell carcinoma.
  • Non-neoplastic isn't always harmless: lichen sclerosus is inflammatory but predisposes to carcinoma. And condyloma acuminatum (HPV 6 and 11) is benign, not premalignant.
  • The uterus: chronic endometritis (plasma cells) is inflammatory; the leiomyoma, very common, is benign, a well-circumscribed muscle nodule that causes abnormal bleeding; the leiomyosarcoma is very aggressive and spreads to the lung.
  • The breast's benign conditions: mastitis, duct ectasia (can retract the nipple) and traumatic fat necrosis.
  • In situ breast lesions, as taught: DCIS needs treatment (surgery, with or without radiotherapy); the WHO now calls LCIS neoplastic but benign, with no treatment needed.
  • Paget disease of the nipple (scaly, red) is a carcinoma, usually with one in the breast beneath it, so the breast is imaged. Invasive carcinomas: ductal forms glands; lobular grows in single files, without glands.
