Watch for: In "select the neoplastic lesions", the decoys are atrophic vaginitis, Candida vaginitis and lichen simplex chronicus. The hub's chart puts condyloma with the non-neoplastic lesions, as a benign HPV lesion; no question asks which side. LCIS: the questions follow the lecture (benign, no treatment; DCIS is the one treated), though textbooks also call LCIS a marker of higher breast cancer risk, followed with surveillance. Said not needed: telling DCIS from LCIS under the microscope.

items.h: Important infectious causes of reproductive tract disease
items.body:
The infections to know are the vaginitis pair, Candida and Trichomonas, each recognized in cytology by its own look, and HPV, the virus of the whole genital tract in women and men. Tell them from atrophic vaginitis, common in older women and not an infection.

Know this
  • Candida, a fungus: pseudohyphae that look like "little sticks" in the cytology, with a lot of inflammation; very frequent.
  • Trichomonas vaginalis: a sexually transmitted protozoan, a very common cause of vaginitis; it looks like a squamous cell with cytoplasmic prolongations (pseudopods).
  • Atrophic vaginitis: non-infectious, very common in older women; no organism.
  • HPV infects the genital tract of women and men: 6 and 11 (low risk) cause the benign condyloma acuminatum; 16 and 18 (high risk) the premalignant squamous intraepithelial lesions and carcinomas. Its mark: the koilocyte.
  • The vulva's infections are the same ones that affect the vagina, the cervix and the male genital tract.
  • Chronic endometritis: plasma cells in the endometrial stroma; a very common, easily treated cause of infertility in a healthy-looking woman; antibiotics.
  • Mastitis: during breastfeeding, skin bacteria climb the lactiferous ducts; very painful; antibiotics.

Watch for: The wrong choices swap these clues: prolongations are Trichomonas, little sticks Candida, a halo around the nucleus HPV. Trichomonas is the sexually transmitted one. The lichens are inflammatory, not infectious.

items.h: Relationship between HPV and cervical neoplasia
items.body:
Cervical cancer starts where the cervix's two linings meet, the transformation zone, because their constant "fight" keeps it inflamed and open to HPV. High-risk HPV causes the precursor lesions, which the Pap test finds by their koilocytes, so screening and the vaccine can prevent the cancer.

Know this
  • Endocervix: mucinous glandular (columnar), red. Ectocervix: non-keratinizing squamous, white.
  • The transformation zone is their junction, where the epithelia collide, "the fighting of epithelia." It is constantly inflamed and injured, so open to infection, above all HPV, and it is where cervical cancer arises.
  • The precursors: squamous intraepithelial lesions (SIL; CIN). Low grade progress slowly and can regress; high grade are less likely to regress and more likely to progress.
  • About 90 percent are linked to HPV, in the reproductive years; the high-risk types are 16 and 18.
  • The koilocyte, HPV's cytopathic effect: a bigger nucleus with a clear halo around it (a true cavity). Cytology looks for it in a Pap smear; biopsies show it too.
  • High grade: crowding, hyperchromasia, loss of maturation; in cytology, less cytoplasm, a higher nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and pleomorphic nuclei.
  • SILs are in situ; once they invade the stroma, they are squamous cell carcinoma.
  • Cervical cancer is fourth in women worldwide (breast is first), less frequent in the United States thanks to Pap screening, which lowers incidence and mortality; about a fourth of U.S. women lack access.
  • The HPV vaccine lowers the incidence, especially in adolescents, but its full benefit may take decades. Management is now risk-based.
Low grade (LSIL)High grade (HSIL)

Watch for: Low grade regresses, high grade progresses, not the reverse. HPV 6 and 11 don't cause the high-grade lesions. Screening, not the vaccine, explains the lower U.S. rate. A Pap smear shows cells, not invasion. Said not needed: the screening slide's details.

items.h: Important age-related patterns of reproductive tract tumors
items.body:
Age is a strong clue: a primitive sarcoma in a little girl, HPV-driven squamous carcinomas in the reproductive years, and in older women the vulvar carcinoma of lichen sclerosus and the aggressive endometrial carcinoma. "Know that there are certain tumors that affect the girls, and usually the squamous cell carcinomas affect the women in reproductive age."

Know this
  • Girls under 5: sarcoma botryoides of the vagina, an embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, very primitive (it can show as vaginal bleeding and a grape-like mass). A good prognosis if found in time and treated with surgery and chemotherapy.
  • Reproductive age: the squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and vagina, with their HPV-linked precursors.
  • Endometrioid adenocarcinoma: younger (pre- or perimenopausal) women with estrogen excess (obesity, estrogen without progesterone); it resembles endometrium, well differentiated, less aggressive.
  • Over 65, postmenopausal: the other endometrial carcinoma, unlike endometrium and more aggressive.
  • Over 60: the HPV-independent vulvar squamous cell carcinoma, from lichen sclerosus.
  • Also in older women: an endometrial polyp can be the source of a carcinoma, so it is sampled entirely.

Watch for: Sarcoma botryoides is a little girls' tumor that does well when treated in time. The estrogen-driven endometrioid type is the less aggressive one of younger women; the aggressive type is the older women's. Leiomyomas are very common, but no question keys their age.

The single one that leads to carcinoma: the HPV-independent vulvar squamous cell carcinoma of older women.
A benign, sexually transmitted, finger-like, wart-like lesion anywhere on the anogenital tract, from HPV 6 and 11, the low-risk types; koilocytes under the microscope.
An embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma of the vagina in girls under 5, a very primitive tumor with a good prognosis if found in time and treated with surgery and chemotherapy.

Human papillomavirus, which infects the whole genital tract of women and men. Types 6 and 11 (low risk) cause condylomas; 16 and 18 (high risk) cause the squamous intraepithelial lesions and carcinomas. Its mark on a cell is the koilocyte.

The squamous intraepithelial lesions (CIN) of the transformation zone, about 90 percent HPV-linked: low grade can regress, high grade tends to progress. They are in situ until they invade the stroma as squamous cell carcinoma.

Vaginal inflammation from Candida (a fungus: pseudohyphae, "little sticks") or Trichomonas vaginalis (a sexually transmitted protozoan with cytoplasmic prolongations). Atrophic vaginitis of older women is the non-infectious kind.
